note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Wang Saffron Park Hospital Saffron Park, London, E14 7JL Dear Dr Wang John Doe, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: P546484 NHS No. 5484656746 Flat 15 Roundwood Road, London, E14 7JL Thank you for asking me to review your patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He lives in supported accommodation where rotating staff maintain daily seizure charts, which we used as the primary source for today’s assessment. Since his last review here in March 2025, the charts and his account suggest a fluctuating pattern with brief episodes most days. On the accommodation logs, the observed frequency is noted as ≤ four per day, with variable clustering, often in the late afternoon or evening. Staff describe sudden behavioural arrest with unresponsiveness and occasional limb stiffening lasting under a minute, followed by brief confusion; he does not recall most events and there are no clear injuries reported. No consistent triggers have been identified, though poor sleep and missed meals are sometimes noted beforehand. He has not driven. Medication adherence is generally good according to the blister pack returns. He is currently on Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He reports intermittent daytime fatigue and mild low mood, which he attributes to broken sleep on busy nights in the residence. There have been no rashes, hyponatraemia symptoms, or clear cognitive decline reported by staff. We discussed care coordination with the accommodation team. I have provided them with a simplified event documentation template and asked that they continue the daily charting and note any injuries, prolonged events (>5 minutes), or need for rescue medication. I have also requested they document sleep hours and mealtime regularity alongside events to explore potential associations. Plan agreed today: - Continue current anti-seizure regimen unchanged for now while we collect a further four weeks of structured logs from the supported accommodation team. - Arrange a routine EEG and repeat bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) to coincide with his next clinic visit. - Provide the patient with information on sleep hygiene and stress management strategies; he felt these were acceptable. - I will review him again in 8–10 weeks with the updated charts and test results. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 30 May 2016 Dr Anita Kerr Riverside Medical Centre 22 Riverside Walk, London, SE10 9AB Dear Dr Anita Kerr Michael Carter, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H837294 NHS No. 7845632190 Flat 3, 14 Millstream Court, London, SE10 8PT I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. As you know he has generalised epilepsy. Since my last assessment he reports a variable pattern of episodes but overall a frequency of ≤ four seizures per week, typically brief generalised convulsions or absence episodes as described below. He has maintained good adherence to medication and has been keeping a diary which corroborates this frequency. He describes two main event types: (1) abrupt loss of awareness with eyelid fluttering and brief behavioural arrest lasting 10–20 seconds, occurring in clusters on stressful days; and (2) generalised tonic–clonic seizures, usually from wakefulness, lasting around 60–90 seconds with post‑ictal fatigue and myalgia. There have been no focal warning symptoms, tongue biting is occasional, and injuries have been minor (one bruised shoulder last month). There is no clear menstrual or sleep‑deprivation trigger; however, he notes that missed meals and high caffeine intake may precipitate events. Family members have witnessed several episodes and confirm generalised onset without lateralising features. Past antiseizure medication side effects have been documented historically, including a pruritic rash with Lamotrigine (resolved on cessation) and gastrointestinal upset with Valproate (nausea and dyspepsia at higher doses). He is currently taking Levetiracetam 1 g b.d. and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He reports mild irritability on Levetiracetam that is tolerable and denies current rash, visual disturbance, or significant gastrointestinal symptoms. No recent hospital admissions. He does not drive. Examination today was unremarkable with normal cognition, intact cranial nerves, and no focal neurological deficits. Weight and metabolic observations are stable. Previous EEG demonstrated generalised spike‑and‑wave discharges consistent with a generalised epilepsy syndrome; MRI brain (last year) was normal. Plan: We discussed ongoing self‑management and recording of events. Given the present pattern of ≤ four seizures per week and acceptable tolerability, he prefers to continue current therapy for now while we complete repeat EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation to re‑assess generalised activity. I have arranged this for the next available slot and requested medication levels and routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) to ensure no biochemical contributors. We also reviewed safety, seizure first aid, and avoidance of identified precipitants. He is aware of SUDEP information resources. Follow‑up is planned in 4 months, with earlier review if the frequency increases or new adverse effects occur. Yours sincerely

Patel Mr Daniel Hughes, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: H928374 NHS No. 8473926150 Flat 3, 29 Fleet Street, London EC4Y 1AA Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy type – patient reports features of both generalised seizures (brief absences and occasional generalised tonic–clonic events) and focal aware/aware-impaired episodes with temporal features. Seizure frequency currently reported as ≤ 6 to 7 per year, typically clustering around periods of jet lag and sleep loss related to frequent business travel across time zones. Appointments are often conducted by telephone due to travel schedule. MRI brain (2018): structurally normal; no definite epileptogenic lesion identified. EEG (2020, routine): generalised spike–wave activity with intermittent left temporal sharp waves; photic stimulation unremarkable. Previous medication: Sodium valproate (weight gain, tremor), carbamazepine (dizziness, hyponatraemia), levetiracetam (mood irritability), clobazam PRN for travel-related clusters, lamotrigine (partial benefit), lacosamide (no clear benefit), topiramate (cognitive slowing), zonisamide (insomnia), perampanel (mood change). Not taken: brivaracetam, cenobamate, eslicarbazepine, rufinamide, vigabatrin, tiagabine, pregabalin, primidone. Comorbidities: Migraine without aura (stress/sleep-loss related). No known cardiac disease. No history of status epilepticus. I reviewed Mr Daniel Hughes via a scheduled telephone clinic today, as he is currently travelling for work. He reports his seizure burden remains ≤ 6 to 7 per year, with a recognisable pattern: brief focal aware episodes with déjà vu and epigastric rising lasting under a minute, and rarer generalised tonic–clonic seizures typically following multiple long-haul flights. He describes occasional brief absences noted by colleagues during videoconferences. He keeps a diary correlating events with irregular sleep, overnight flights, and caffeine excess. No injuries. No hospital admissions since last review. Current medicines: - Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily - Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily (initiated abroad three months ago; self-reported better tolerability than levetiracetam) - Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for travel weeks (1–3 nights around long-haul flights) - Riboflavin 200 mg daily for migraine prophylaxis (self-initiated) Travel and lifestyle context: Works across Europe, the US, and Asia with frequent time zone shifts. Uses airline pre-boarding to reduce stress, wears medical ID, and adheres to local driving restrictions when abroad. Reports good medication adherence using phone reminders, but missed two doses in the last quarter during a delayed connection. Sleep remains irregular on multi-sector trips. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine and brivaracetam at current doses given tolerability and seizure frequency of ≤ 6 to 7 per year. Reinforced adherence strategies during flight disruptions (carry-on blister packs, duplicate alarm prompts, and setting local-time conversion reminders). - Clobazam PRN limited to travel-associated high-risk periods; advised on sedation risk and avoidance of alcohol when used. - Agreed to trial structured sleep hygiene across time zones (patient-led): maintaining dark/light cues, limiting late caffeine, and scheduling short naps on arrival days based on local time; patient prefers non-pharmacological measures. - Safety: reiterated water precautions, working at height, and local regulations for driving post-seizure when abroad; patient confirms compliance. - Investigations: No immediate further imaging required. If breakthrough frequency increases or semiology changes, consider prolonged ambulatory EEG to characterise both generalised and focal events during travel periods. - Follow-up: Telephone review in 4 months or earlier if two or more events occur within a month. Patient will forward seizure diary screenshots monthly via secure portal. Thank you for your ongoing care and for assisting with prescription continuity while he is overseas. Please contact me if any issues arise. Yours sincerely

Reynolds Consultant Neurologist, Sarah Thompson, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: KCH728415 NHS No. 9075634218 12 Willow Crescent, London, SE15 2AB Thank you for asking me to review your patient. I am pleased to report a sustained improvement in their overall stability and day‑to‑day functioning. The patient describes a calmer routine over recent months, with structured rest periods and regular time away from usual stressors. Travel and time set aside for relaxation were noted by the patient to improve general wellbeing; this is recorded here neutrally as part of the history. By way of comparison, prior to this period the seizures were occurring every 1 or 2 weeks. Over the past year, however, the patient and family report that events have become markedly infrequent, such that the current pattern is ≤ two or four per year. This has translated into fewer unscheduled contacts and quicker return to baseline after brief episodes of disorientation. There have been no injuries, no hospital attendances, and no changes in speech, focal weakness, or memory beyond a short-lived post-event tiredness lasting minutes to an hour at most. Medication has remained unchanged, with good adherence reported. Sleep hygiene and pacing strategies have been continued. There is no recent intercurrent illness, no alcohol or substance use, and no clear precipitating factors identified. The patient keeps a simple diary, which aligns with the impression above. Examination in clinic today was unremarkable with stable observations, normal gait, and no lateralising neurological signs. On balance, the clinical picture is of gradual improvement with a materially reduced event burden to ≤ two or four per year, compared with the earlier pattern of seizures every 1 or 2 weeks. I have advised continuation of the current approach and to maintain a consistent routine. The patient will continue to document any events and will let us know if there is any change in frequency, severity, or recovery pattern. I will plan routine follow‑up in six months, with earlier review if needed. Please do not hesitate to contact me if there are any concerns or if further information would be helpful. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Helen Armitage Royal London Hospital Department of Neurology, Whitechapel Road, London E1 1FR Dear Dr Helen Armitage, John Smith, DOB: 11-07-1984, Hospital No: S845921 NHS No. 7823495610 34 Kensington Road, London, W8 5NP Diagnoses: - Focal epilepsy with focal aware seizures and occasional focal to bilateral tonic-clonic evolution - History of childhood febrile seizures (resolved) - MRI brain (August 2025): Subtle left mesial temporal sclerosis - EEG (July 2025): Interictal left temporal sharp waves Current Medication: - Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd - Lacosamide 100 mg bd - Midazolam 10 mg buccal, as rescue for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) Plan: - Optimise anti-seizure medication: increase Lacosamide to 150 mg bd over two weeks if tolerated - Continue Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd - Seizure diary to closely track frequency and potential triggers - Driving: patient not currently driving; to follow DVLA guidance and remain off driving until seizure-free per regulations - Consider referral to the epilepsy surgery MDT if disabling seizures persist despite optimisation - Safety advice provided regarding bathing, heights, hot surfaces, and nocturnal supervision I reviewed John in clinic today regarding focal epilepsy. He describes brief focal aware seizures characterised by rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, and transient speech arrest, occasionally followed by right-hand automatisms and, more rarely, progression to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. He reports a current seizure frequency of 17 per month, typically clustering around periods of sleep deprivation and high work-related stress. He has found avoidance of alcohol helpful and is now using a structured sleep schedule. There is a remote history of childhood febrile seizures without neurological sequelae. Adult-onset focal seizures began in late 2023. Prior trials included Lamotrigine up to 200 mg bd, which was discontinued due to rash, and Carbamazepine up to 600 mg bd, which reduced frequency but caused significant dizziness and hyponatraemia; both medications were stopped in consultation with his previous team. We discussed treatment options. Given the MRI and EEG concordance suggesting a left mesial temporal focus, I have recommended optimising current therapy by titrating Lacosamide to 150 mg twice daily if tolerated, while continuing Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. He will maintain a detailed seizure diary and track potential triggers. A rescue plan using buccal Midazolam for prolonged seizures was reinforced. If disabling seizures persist at a rate similar to the current 17 per month despite dose optimisation and adherence, I will refer him to the epilepsy surgery multidisciplinary team for further evaluation, including consideration of prolonged video-EEG telemetry and neuropsychological assessment. We also reviewed DVLA regulations; he is not currently driving and understands requirements for resumption. I will review him again in three months, or earlier if there is any deterioration or adverse effects from the dose increase. With best wishes,

note_text_single_line: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 01 June 2020 Dr Priya Nair Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy Kingsway Community Hospital, London Dear Dr Priya Nair, Ms Aisha Rahman, DOB: 22-08-1992, Hospital No: K847203 NHS No. 9083175621 Flat 12, 4 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3QH Diagnosis: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy, with generalised tonic–clonic seizures occurring from sleep and focal aware auras occasionally progressing to focal impaired awareness events. Aetiology: No definitive structural lesion identified on MRI; family history of seizures in a first-degree relative reported. EEG with mixed features including generalised spike–wave and independent right temporal sharp activity. Other Medical Problems: Mild asthma on inhaled corticosteroid as required. Vitamin D insufficiency previously treated, currently stable. Management Plan: - Continue sodium valproate modified-release 500 mg mane and 1,000 mg nocte. - Maintain clobazam 10 mg nocte as adjunct for nocturnal generalised seizures. - Rescue plan discussed: buccal midazolam 10 mg for prolonged generalised tonic–clonic seizure (>5 minutes) or seizure clustering, with instructions provided to family. - Driving advice reiterated in accordance with DVLA guidance for combined seizure types; patient has self-declared and remains off driving pending seizure control. - Lifestyle: reinforce regular sleep, hydration, and avoidance of known precipitants (patient-reported missed meals and sleep deprivation). - Review in four months with repeat trough valproate level and LFTs prior to clinic; consider lacosamide add-on if focal impaired awareness events persist. Clinical Summary: Since the last review, Ms Aisha Rahman reports that events tend to cluster every seven to nine days. On those days, they experience a brief focal aware aura described in their own words as a “tight, metallic taste with a rising flutter in the stomach and a momentary pull to the right side,” lasting 10–20 seconds. They have practiced aura recognition strategies previously and now routinely sit down, slow their breathing, and alert a family member when the warning occurs. This has reduced secondary generalisation on several occasions. Over the same interval, there have been two nocturnal generalised tonic–clonic seizures, each under two minutes, with typical post-ictal confusion and myalgia but no injury. Daytime focal impaired awareness episodes are rare and usually follow the described warning if they cannot implement their strategy in time. No adverse effects from current medication are reported beyond mild morning sedation, which is acceptable to the patient. Weight is stable; mood is good without features of depression or anxiety. There is no new neurological deficit on examination. We discussed trigger recognition and the patient prioritised consistent sleep and regular meals; they have set phone reminders and are keeping a seizure diary correlating auras, full seizures, and potential triggers. Family have been re-educated in the rescue plan and recovery position. I will continue to support their self-management approach, given the usefulness of early warning recognition in reducing generalisation. No further investigations requested today beyond routine blood monitoring for valproate. I have provided a work letter confirming variable fatigue every seven to nine days corresponding to their seizure pattern and the need for flexible start times after nocturnal events. Yours sincerely

No rashes, no cognitive complaints, and no new neurological symptoms were reported. Assessment: Her description of brief focal aware episodes (epigastric rising sensation and déjà vu) occasionally progressing to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures is in keeping with focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Despite optimised adherence, the overall seizure burden has not changed; specifically, she has had two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months. There is no clear diurnal pattern. She denies alcohol excess and recreational drug use. Sleep is variable due to shift work, which may be a contributory factor. Plan: • Continue current antiseizure medications at the present doses, as there has been no deterioration but also no improvement in the count of two drop attacks and five tonic-clonic in the past three months. • Arrange MRI brain with epilepsy protocol (3T) and repeat EEG with sleep deprivation to refine localisation. • Provide written advice on sleep hygiene and seizure triggers; patient will review feasibility of reducing night shifts with her employer. • Safety counselled regarding drop attacks and convulsive seizures at home and in public; discussed SUDEP awareness and first-aid guidance with her and her partner. • Driving: she has already informed the DVLA and is not driving. Follow-up: We will review her in clinic in four months or sooner if events escalate, injuries occur, or medication side effects emerge. Yours sincerely,

No adverse effects reported beyond mild initial fatigue which has since settled. Rescue medication not currently prescribed. History and current status: Jordan Ellis works full-time on the gate line at a busy metropolitan station where prolonged standing, loud announcements, and intermittent crowd surges are routine. Over the review interval, they report 1 - 10 focal aware seizures during the last two months. These events typically last 30–60 seconds, with preserved awareness, a rising epigastric sensation, brief right-hand tingling, and occasional déjà vu. There is no loss of consciousness, falls, or post-event confusion. Episodes are more likely during late shifts after consecutive long days or when managing sudden influxes of passengers. No clear alcohol excess or sleep deprivation beyond shift-related variability. No recent head injury. Workplace context: They have adopted informal strategies at work such as stepping back from the barrier line and signalling colleagues when the aura begins. They report that bright LED signage and continuous standing near the ticket gates may act as non-specific stressors. They remain fit for duties from their perspective, as the events are brief and fully aware, but they would value a formal occupational health review to consider adjustments (e.g. scheduled micro-breaks, rotation away from peak surge periods) to reduce triggers. Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily. If the frequency increases or new features emerge (loss of awareness, injury, or generalisation), we will consider dose optimisation after serum level review and discuss alternative agents if needed. - Provide a brief written summary for occupational health outlining the brief, aware nature of events and typical precipitating circumstances, at the patient’s request. - Safety counselling reinforced regarding working near moving crowds and the importance of adequate rest between shifts. Driving advice remains per DVLA standards for their current event profile. - Arrange routine EEG and updated MRI as part of ongoing evaluation. Follow-up: We will review in clinic in four months, sooner if there is any deterioration or change in semiology. Yours sincerely

Current symptoms and functional status: - Occasional aura-like sensations precede the monthly event; no confusional state or automatisms reported since adopting the new routine. - Headaches are infrequent and responsive to simple analgesia. Medication history (patient-reported): - Previously used: levetiracetam (fatigue, limited benefit), clobazam (daytime sedation), carbamazepine, valproate, phenytoin, phenobarbital, gabapentin, vigabatrin, lacosamide. - Not taken to date: topiramate, zonisamide, pregabalin, tiagabine, acetazolamide, perampanel, retigabine, rufinamide, primidone. - Current regular medicines: lamotrigine 150 mg morning, 100 mg afternoon, 100 mg evening; folic acid 5 mg daily; occasional metoclopramide for intermittent nausea. Plan discussed today: - Given the clear improvement associated with retirement and a steady routine, we agreed on continued observation without immediate medication changes. Yours sincerely,

note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Priya Anand Holloway Road Health Centre 192 Holloway Road London N7 8DL Dear Dr Priya Anand Jordan Patel, DOB: 14-03-1990, Hospital No: H937214 NHS No. 7843206159 Flat 12, 6 Arterton Close, London N1 0PH Diagnoses/summary: Focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe onset. Ketogenic/modified diet: Patient is following a supervised modified ketogenic diet (external provider). Recorded plan: 3:1 fat-to-combined protein/carbohydrate ratio; carbohydrate limited to approximately 20–25 g/day; fluid intake target 2.0–2.5 L/day; medium-chain triglyceride oil 15 mL with breakfast and evening meal; vitamin/mineral supplementation as per diet protocol (multivitamin, selenium 55 mcg/day, vitamin D3 1000 IU/day). Diet initiated March 2025; monitored by dietetics team elsewhere with monthly telehealth reviews. Patient reports improved alertness in the morning and reduced post-event fatigue, but seizure frequency remains at convulsion weekly. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily - Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily - Folic acid 5 mg once daily - Omeprazole 20 mg once daily (dyspepsia) Previous medication trials (ineffective or poorly tolerated): Carbamazepine (dizziness), valproate (weight gain, mood), lacosamide (somnolence), clobazam PRN (sedation), gabapentin (no benefit). No history of topiramate, zonisamide, perampanel, or pregabalin. Allergies: No known drug allergies. History since last review: I saw the patient today unaccompanied. They report adherence to both medicines and diet with a written log. Typical focal onset features include epigastric rising sensation, brief speech arrest, and right facial automatisms, evolving on occasion to bilateral tonic–clonic activity. The overall pattern over the past two months has been stable at convulsion weekly, usually in the late evening, with post-ictal confusion lasting 30–45 minutes. There have been no injuries, tongue biting once in August, and no prolonged events requiring rescue therapy. No clear dietary triggers identified; sleep curtailment and high work stress appear to lower threshold per patient account. They continue to drive abstinent in line with DVLA regulations (self-reported). Mood is described as “variable but manageable”; no suicidal ideation; screening scores with the diet team reportedly low. Weight has fallen by 3.2 kg since commencing the modified ketogenic plan; hydration is reportedly adequate. Examination: BP 118/72, pulse 72 regular, weight 68.5 kg (down from 71.7 kg in March). Neurological examination non-focal. No cutaneous stigmata. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations unremarkable. Investigations: Historical MRI (report from 2016) described as non-lesional. Prior EEGs have shown left temporal interictal discharges per patient report; we do not yet have the raw data or formal reports from the external centre. Routine bloods requested today (U&E, LFT, FBC, vitamin D, lipid profile, bicarbonate) to monitor dietary effects and antiepileptic drug safety. Assessment: Focal epilepsy with likely temporal lobe onset events continuing at convulsion weekly despite dual therapy and a supervised modified ketogenic diet. Some symptomatic gains reported (energy, shorter recovery) but no clear reduction in convulsive frequency. No red flags elicited today. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine and levetiracetam at current doses for now; confirm trough levels are not required by current protocol. - Obtain formal copies of prior MRI and EEG reports; consider repeat video-EEG telemetry if events remain unchanged over the next 4–6 months. - Liaise (with patient consent) with the external ketogenic/modified diet team to share outcomes data and blood results; keep current macronutrient targets unchanged pending labs. - Safety: reinforced seizure first aid and SUDEP risk discussion; patient to avoid swimming alone and heights; continue to follow DVLA guidance. - Lifestyle: maintain regular sleep schedule; patient will keep a detailed seizure and diet diary noting sleep, stress, and timing relative to meals. - Follow-up: nurse-led telephone review in 6 weeks to check events, tolerance, and lab results; clinic review in 4 months or sooner if convulsions cluster, injuries occur, or prolonged events develop. Thank you for your ongoing care and for forwarding any interim concerns. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 21 September 2025 Dr Amelia Fraser Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Amelia Fraser Consultant Neurologist, Jonathan Pierce, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: KCH482917 NHS No. 9473201856 12 Bracken Close, Sydenham, London SE26 4HP Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw today with his partner. He reports a remote history of mild traumatic brain injury in his early twenties without documented loss of consciousness beyond a brief daze, and no neurosurgical intervention. There is no known family history of seizure disorders. He does not drink alcohol to excess and denies recreational drug use. Sleep has been fragmented recently due to early work starts. He describes daily events despite treatment trials in primary care. The typical episodes are reported as brief loss of awareness with stiffening and subsequent generalised shaking, sometimes preceded by a rising internal sensation and a metallic taste. His partner has witnessed several events and timed them at around 60–90 seconds, followed by tiredness and headache for up to an hour. He keeps a diary and notes TC one/d over the past month, with only two seizure-free days in that period. He has had two minor tongue bites but no significant injuries. There is no consistent morning predominance; they occur at variable times, including at work and at home. There is no clear catamenial pattern (not applicable), and no definite photic provocation. Current medications: levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily, lamotrigine titrating currently at 50 mg twice daily; sertraline 50 mg once daily for mood. No known drug allergies. He has previously tried sodium valproate briefly but discontinued after weight gain and tremor. He reports good adherence, and his partner corroborates this. No recent intercurrent illness. He is not driving. On examination today, he was alert and orientated with normal language and cranial nerve function. Motor, coordination, and gait were within normal limits. No focal neurological deficits were identified. Vital signs were stable. Investigations to date: basic bloods last month (FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, HbA1c, B12, folate, TSH) were within reference ranges. An MRI brain from 2019 (non-epilepsy protocol) was reported as normal. He has not had prolonged EEG monitoring; a routine EEG five years ago was normal. Given the ongoing daily events (TC one/d) and the remote head injury, I discussed the value of updated epilepsy-protocol MRI and prolonged video-EEG monitoring to characterise the events and correlate semiology with electrographic findings. He is agreeable to proceeding. We also discussed general measures including regular sleep, hydration, and stress management as supportive strategies, and the importance of medication adherence, which he and his partner already prioritise. Plan: - Arrange video-EEG monitoring (inpatient if feasible) to capture typical events. - Request epilepsy-protocol MRI brain. - Continue current medication regimen pending further data; liaise with pharmacy to ensure uninterrupted supply. - Seizure diary to be maintained, including possible triggers and timing. - Provide workplace letter regarding safety considerations; he is currently not driving and understands DVLA requirements following seizures. - Review in clinic after investigations or sooner if there is any escalation (prolonged events >5 minutes, clusters without recovery, or injury). Many thanks for your referral. I will update you following the investigations. Yours sincerely

He reports no recent head injuries, medication non-adherence, or sleep deprivation beyond occasional broken sleep related to shift work. Since I last saw him in May 2016, he has kept an updated paper log. Seizure: 2016: May x1, Jun x1, Jul x0, Aug x1, Sep x0, Oct x1, Nov x0. He describes his typical events as focal aware seizures with a rising epigastric sensation and brief speech arrest lasting 30–60 seconds, without loss of awareness, followed occasionally (approximately once every 2–3 months) by focal impaired-awareness episodes with automatisms and post-event fatigue for up to an hour. He denies any generalised convulsions this year. Current treatment: Carbamazepine modified-release 400 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. He reports good adherence, no rash, no diplopia, and only mild intermittent dizziness when dehydrated. No mood deterioration on Levetiracetam by his account. He does not drive and remains compliant with DVLA guidance. Examination today was unremarkable. Neurological examination was normal with no focal deficits. Weight and blood pressure stable. Routine bloods from September 2016 (U&E, LFT, FBC) were within normal limits. He brings his original paper calendars, which corroborate the above frequency and provide consistent timing patterns (late evening predominance on days following consecutive night shifts). Plan: Given the relative stability with focal seizures largely brief and aware, and no generalised events, I have not altered medication today. We discussed sleep hygiene and maintaining consistent dosing times. He will continue to use his paper seizure calendar and bring this to follow-up. I have requested a repeat Carbamazepine level and routine bloods via your surgery in 8–10 weeks, mainly for monitoring. If the frequency increases (two or more focal impaired-awareness events in a month) he will contact the clinic for earlier review. I will review him again in six months, sooner if needed. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Aisha Rahman St Thomas’ Hospital Department of Neurology, Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7EH Dear Dr Aisha Rahman, Michael Turner, DOB: 14-02-1990, Hospital No: L937521 NHS No. 9064157823 12 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3JP Diagnoses: - Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy) - MRI brain (March 2024): left mesial temporal sclerosis - EEG (April 2024): generalised spike–wave bursts with independent left temporal sharp waves Current Medication: - Levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily - Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily - Rescue: Buccal midazolam 10 mg as per care plan Plan: - Urgent admission today for stabilisation in view of nineteen episode of status epilepticus in the past week and inadequate response to current regimen - Commence sodium valproate loading and maintenance if no contraindications; continue levetiracetam and lamotrigine pending inpatient review - Optimise rescue plan and provide written safety leaflet; liaise with community epilepsy specialist nurse - Seizure diary app data to be exported to EHR and used to guide treatment adjustments - DVLA advice reinforced: must not drive and to notify DVLA I reviewed Michael Turner in my clinic today, accompanied by his partner. He uses a seizure diary app which syncs with his wearable; the entries were reviewed during the consultation. Over the last seven days the diary documents nineteen episode of status epilepticus in the past week, each defined in the app by continuous convulsive activity exceeding five minutes or repeated focal-to-bilateral tonic–clonic events without full recovery. Several events began with a focal impaired-awareness semiology (right facial twitching, speech arrest, manual automatisms) progressing to generalised tonic–clonic seizures. There were also brief absence-like events recorded on two mornings. Triggers noted by the patient include sleep deprivation and a recent viral illness. Medication adherence is reported as high, with app reminders confirming on-time dosing for the past month. Buccal midazolam was administered three times at home per the rescue plan, with partial effect. This pattern is consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy, supported by prior EEG findings of generalised spike–wave activity alongside left temporal sharp waves, and MRI evidence of left mesial temporal sclerosis. Given the recent escalation, breakthrough clusters, and prolonged seizures despite dual therapy, I consider him unstable for outpatient management and have arranged urgent admission via the Same Day Emergency Care pathway for monitoring, intravenous therapy as needed, anti-seizure medication optimisation, and review of precipitating factors (infection screen, metabolic profile, and consideration of status protocol). The inpatient team will upload the last 30 days of seizure diary app logs to the record to assist titration and timing of dosing. We discussed safety: supervision when bathing, avoiding heights and open water, adherence to the rescue protocol, and ensuring midazolam is in-date and immediately accessible. I advised strict sleep hygiene and infection management. Driving restrictions were explained; he understands that he must not drive and must inform the DVLA. Occupational and social support will be coordinated through the epilepsy specialist nurse. I will arrange a multidisciplinary review following discharge to consider longer-term options including valproate-based therapy if tolerated, and, depending on response, possible evaluation for epilepsy surgery or neuromodulation given the focal onset component. I will update you following his inpatient stay. Please contact me if further information is required. With best wishes,

note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr R Patel Maple Grove Medical Centre 45 Maple Grove, London, SE5 2DL Dear Dr R Patel Michael Green, DOB: 14-03-1990, Hospital No: H824559 NHS No. 7392018465 12A Brookside Court, Peckham, London, SE15 4HT I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He is known to have a history of childhood febrile seizures, with no documented events in adolescence, and has presented in adulthood with recurrent seizures. He reports that over the past week he experienced three - five episode of status epilepticus in the past week, necessitating attendance at the Emergency Department on two occasions where episodes terminated following intravenous therapy. He describes preceding hours of mounting anxiety, disturbed sleep, and missed meals due to shift work. His partner reports prolonged unresponsiveness and generalised stiffening with bilateral jerking movements lasting beyond five minutes on at least two occasions, with post-event confusion and myalgia. He is currently prescribed Levetiracetam 1 g b.d. and Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., which he has generally tolerated; he notes intermittent dizziness and reduced appetite since up-titration last month. He denies new rash, visual disturbance or mood lability beyond situational stress related to work. There is no recent head injury, alcohol excess, or recreational drug use by his account. Sleep is fragmented as he is working alternating night shifts. He uses a smartphone seizure diary and his entries correlate with periods of poor sleep and missed doses. Neurological examination today is non-focal. Cardiovascular and general examination are unremarkable. Routine bloods taken last week by his GP (FBC, U&E, LFTs) were within normal limits by his report; we have requested copies. He has not yet had an MRI brain or prolonged EEG in adulthood. Given the clustering this week and attendance to ED, we discussed emergency care planning, medication adherence, and avoidance of sleep deprivation. He and his partner have been given written advice regarding prolonged seizures and red flag features. He is agreeable to further investigations and to meet our epilepsy specialist nurse for education and support. Plan: - Urgent MRI brain with epilepsy protocol and prolonged video EEG (ambulatory if feasible) to characterise events and guide management. - Serum Levetiracetam and Lamotrigine levels to support adherence assessment; repeat routine bloods including LFTs and bone profile. - Epilepsy Specialist Nurse input for safety counselling, rescue plan reinforcement, and diary review. - Occupational advice: avoid lone working at height or near open water; ensure adequate sleep scheduling; employer letter offered if needed. - We have provided written emergency guidance for prolonged seizures and advised his partner on when to call 999. I will review him in clinic in four weeks or sooner if there are further prolonged events. A copy of this letter will be sent to the patient and the Epilepsy Specialist Nurse. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Emily Rhodes (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 08 February 2022 10:15 To: neuro.epilepsyclinic@nhs.net Cc: Dr Matthew Singh (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Post-partum review and adjustment plan Hi Emily Epilepsy Diagnosis: Focal epilepsy with probable temporal lobe onset Present Medication: 1. Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily 2. Levetiracetam 250 mg in the morning and 500 mg at night Present Seizure Frequency: The patient reports seven to eight absence seizures this quarter, described as brief staring spells with impaired awareness and automatisms, typically clustering in the late evening. These have occurred in the context of post-partum sleep fragmentation over the last six months. There have been no generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Plan of Action: The temporal association with disrupted night-time sleep following childbirth is notable, with the patient reporting frequent awakenings for infant care and overall sleep duration reduced to approximately 4–5 hours per night. She denies medication non-adherence, intercurrent illness, or alcohol intake. Given the pattern of focal impaired awareness events and the absence of clear provoking factors other than sleep disruption, we will aim to optimise therapy while supporting sleep hygiene. 1) Continue lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily. 2) Adjust levetiracetam to 500 mg twice daily to even out peak–trough variability and reduce evening clustering of focal events. The patient has previously tolerated this dose without mood disturbance. 3) Non-pharmacological measures (patient-reported goals): partner-assisted night feeds where possible, scheduled daytime nap when support available, and consistent wind-down routine before 21:30 to reduce sleep-onset latency. 4) Safety counselling reinforced: avoid co-sleeping when drowsy, continue seizure precautions at changing table and bath time, and do not sleep on elevated surfaces with the infant. 5) Arrange an ambulatory EEG if events persist beyond eight weeks despite dose adjustment, to confirm focal onset. If seizures remain frequent, we will consider introducing lacosamide as adjunctive therapy or rationalising levetiracetam depending on tolerance. I have scheduled a follow-up in eight weeks, sooner if seizure frequency increases or if adverse effects occur. With best wishes

note_text_single_line: Centre for Epilepsy Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 05 November 2014 Dr Sarah Langford Consultant Neurologist Centre for Epilepsy St. Michael’s Neurology Unit, Brixton, London Dear Dr Sarah Langford, Aisha Khan, DOB: 22-09-1996, Hospital No: H874320 NHS No. 4098576321 Flat 12, 4 Willow Court, Peckham, London, SE15 3AB Diagnosis: Generalised epilepsy with good response to Valproate; partial benefit from Topiramate; Lamotrigine previously poorly tolerated due to rash. Aetiology: Presumed genetic generalised epilepsy; normal MRI brain; EEG demonstrating generalised 3 Hz spike–wave discharges. Other Medical Problems: Mild asthma managed with as-needed Salbutamol inhaler; vitamin D insufficiency on cholecalciferol 1000 IU daily; no known drug allergies aside from lamotrigine-associated rash. Management Plan: 1) Continue Sodium Valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte. 2) Maintain Topiramate 50 mg nocte as adjunct pending reassessment. 3) Arrange repeat EEG in six months and serum valproate level at next visit. 4) Lifestyle advice discussed, including regular sleep and alcohol moderation; patient to keep a seizure diary. 5) Review in clinic in six months or sooner if breakthrough clusters occur. Over the past four months, the patient reports that the Median inter-seizure interval ≈ three weeks, with shorter absence episodes typically preceding a single GTCS by 24–48 hours. There have been no myoclonic jerks in the mornings for the last eight weeks since titration of nighttime Valproate. Triggers noted by the patient include sleep deprivation during shift work and higher caffeine intake. No injuries, tongue biting only with the last GTCS, and prompt recovery within 30 minutes. Medication adherence is good, with no missed doses reported in the last eight weeks. Valproate has been well tolerated; weight stable and no mood symptoms. Topiramate associated with transient paraesthesia initially, now resolved. The patient drives only with supervision during lessons and has been advised regarding DVLA seizure-free interval requirements; we have reiterated guidance today. We will continue current therapy given recent improvement and the reported stability of the seizure pattern. Should the diary show reduction beyond the current median interval, we will consider cautious Topiramate taper at the next review. The patient understands the plan and agrees. Yours sincerely

Dietary therapy notes (external service): - Regimen: Modified ketogenic approach (approx. 1.5–2:1 fat to combined protein/carbohydrate). - Carbohydrate limit: ~30–40 g/day. - Monitoring: Weekly home capillary ketone checks (typical readings 0.9–1.7 mmol/L). - Electrolytes and lipids reviewed externally in August 2025; patient reports results within advised targets. - Tolerability: Occasional early-morning nausea; managed with fluid intake and adjusted meal timing. - Adherence: Good, with two planned “flex” meals per month agreed with the diet team. She reports taking Levetiracetam as above without missed doses. She maintains a diary app logging sleep, stress, ketone values, and any neurological symptoms; no entries for events since February 2025. No emergency visits. Driving status discussed; she understands to notify authorities should circumstances change. Plan: - Continue current Levetiracetam dose and dietary regimen under the external team’s guidance. - Arrange serum Levetiracetam level and basic metabolic profile locally in 6–8 weeks (to align with diet review). - Provide copy of this letter to the supervising dietitian (with patient consent) to ensure consistent records. - Safety advice reinforced regarding sleep regularity, hydration, and prompt reporting of any breakthrough events. Administrative notes: Patient prefers e-correspondence. Next review in 4–6 months, sooner if clinical change. Yours sincerely

We arranged today’s review accordingly, and she joined the call from home following her latest return from the rig. Diagnosis: She has generalised epilepsy, with a prior history of generalised tonic–clonic seizures and brief morning myoclonic jerks reported before treatment optimisation. She denies any myoclonic jerks on waking, no absence episodes, and no nocturnal events according to her partner. There have been no witnessed injuries, emergency attendances, or missed workdays related to seizures during this period. Medication: Valproate 500 mg twice daily. Triggers and lifestyle: She is adhering to sleep hygiene recommendations during offshore night shifts and has limited caffeine intake. Alcohol intake is minimal when onshore. She uses a seizure diary app synced to her phone and the last recorded event precedes the seizure-free interval as above. Investigations and safety: Previous EEG showed generalised spike–wave discharges consistent with generalised epilepsy; MRI brain was unremarkable. She has completed workplace safety documentation with her employer, who are aware of her condition and rota planning. She confirms no driving given current regulations and will seek advice if circumstances change. Plan: - Continue valproate 500 mg twice daily unchanged. - Maintain seizure diary and offshore medication contingency. - Telephone review in six months to coincide with her next onshore rotation, or earlier if breakthrough events occur. note_text_single_line: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Ahmed St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Ahmed, Jack Morrison, DOB: 12-03-1993, Hospital No: H918204 NHS No. 5839201746 Flat 4, 29 Lantern Court, London, W10 6QP Medication: Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily; rescue midazolam 5 mg buccal as needed for events longer than 3 minutes (not yet used). I reviewed Jack Morrison, a stage lighting technician with frequent exposure to strobe and high-intensity luminaires. He has a diagnosis of focal epilepsy with probable temporal onset, established on clinical grounds with supportive interictal EEG showing left temporal sharp waves. MRI brain previously reported as normal. Since his last visit three months ago, he reports that events have become less frequent on the current dose of levetiracetam. He notes brief focal aware episodes characterised by a rising epigastric sensation and a momentary blanking of conversation, typically lasting 20–40 seconds, occurring about twice weekly. These are most commonly noticed when he dozes in a chair between rigging sessions, i.e. episodes tend to cluster during short daytime rests rather than during full sleep at night. Colleagues have occasionally observed him pause mid-task and stare, without convulsion, and he is consistently able to recall the event afterwards. There have been no generalised tonic–clonic seizures reported. He describes specific triggers around intense lighting rehearsals, especially prolonged exposure to rapid cues and strobes at close range. He now wears tinted lenses during programming runs and has arranged for colleagues to operate strobes when feasible. He remains fully oriented post-event and returns to work duties after a few minutes. No injuries have occurred. Sleep has been somewhat irregular around touring load-ins, and he is working with his manager to improve rest breaks. On examination today he was well, with normal neurological findings. Blood tests last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs) were within reference ranges. Levetiracetam has been tolerated without mood change or irritability. Plan: - Continue levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. If the daytime rest–associated focal aware episodes increase to more than 3 per week or begin to impair safety-critical tasks, we will consider dose escalation to 1,500 mg twice daily after discussion. - Safety at work: he will maintain a seizure diary noting timing relative to brief daytime rests and lighting exposure patterns. He has informed his supervisor, and a colleague remains present during high-intensity strobe testing. - Photosensitivity risk was discussed. While his epilepsy is focal, high-frequency visual stimuli may still lower seizure threshold in some individuals; he will continue practical mitigations (tinted lenses, increased viewing distance, scheduled breaks, and minimising direct strobe alignment during programming). - Driving status and SUDEP counselling previously provided; no change. We will review him again in four months, or sooner if events increase in frequency or evolve in character. Yours sincerely

Previous medication trials: carbamazepine (partial response, dizziness), lamotrigine (rash at 100 mg bd), levetiracetam (irritability), sodium valproate (weight gain; stopped due to family planning counselling), zonisamide (kidney discomfort, discontinued), lacosamide (ongoing seizures), clobazam prn (sedation), topiramate (word-finding difficulty), perampanel (mood change), brivaracetam (minimal benefit). I reviewed Michael Turner in clinic today, attending with his partner. He reports ongoing focal aware and focal impaired-awareness events. Over the last four months he describes a clustering pattern predominantly when he has minor infections or feels run down; he characterises this as "spells flaring when under the weather," and notes that these bursts coincide with colds and disturbed sleep. Between these periods, events are less frequent but not absent. Typical semiology remains an epigastric rising sensation, pause in speech, lip-smacking, and brief confusion lasting 1–2 minutes, with post-event fatigue for up to an hour. No clear injuries. Last generalised tonic-clonic seizure was 14 months ago after a night shift. Current medication: - Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily - Clobazam 5–10 mg at bedtime as required (uses up to 2–3 nights/week) - Salbutamol inhaler prn - Vitamin D 1000 IU daily Adverse effects: feels slightly flat in mood on higher doses of brivaracetam; otherwise tolerating regimen. Given his prior partial response to sodium channel agents and mood sensitivity to certain drugs, we agreed to trial eslicarbazepine as adjunctive therapy. - Start eslicarbazepine 400 mg nocte for 2 weeks, then increase to 800 mg nocte if tolerated. Continue brivaracetam 100 mg bd. Reduce clobazam prn to the lowest effective use. Side effects discussed (hyponatraemia, rash, dizziness, rare cardiac conduction effects). We will check U&Es (including sodium) at baseline and after dose escalation. - Bloods requested today: U&Es, LFTs, FBC, vitamin D re-check. - Seizure action plan updated. Emphasised sleep regularity, hydration, and prompt management of minor infections as he tends to have "flare-ups during bouts of being unwell." Provided a brief written plan for GP regarding early symptomatic treatment of upper respiratory infections and advice on avoiding interacting medications where possible. - Discussed surgical pathway and neuromodulation. Given MRI-negative status but consistent temporal semiology, we will reconsider advanced evaluation if seizures persist despite two further adequate trials. For now, he prefers to proceed with medication changes. - DVLA guidance reinforced; he remains off driving. - Follow-up: Nurse specialist telephone review in 4–6 weeks to assess tolerability and sodium results; clinic review in 4 months or earlier if deterioration. Thank you for your ongoing care, including support with blood tests and prescription continuation if tolerated and beneficial. Yours sincerely

Over the last six months he describes more rapid-onset events with left facial pulling followed by jerking of the left arm, preserved awareness, then brief speech arrest. note_text_single_line: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel South Thames Neurology Service Neurosciences Department, St George’s Hospital, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Patel, Emily Johnson, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H593742 NHS No. 9473625180 12 Rowan Mews, Croydon, CR0 6LP Diagnoses: Seizure disorder, classification not established. I reviewed Emily Johnson today in the neurology clinic with her partner present. Over the past three months there has been a clear escalation in event burden, best described as a postnatal-related rise in event frequency, compared to her prior stable period. She reports clusters now occurring several times per week, with a shorter prodrome and faster progression than previously noted. The events are disproportionately triggered in environments with intense lighting and high ambient noise (for example, stage rigging during theatre set‑ups and on a factory floor), where she describes a rapid onset of disorientation, speech arrest, and subsequent loss of awareness within 10–20 seconds. Recovery is slower, with post‑event fatigue and headache lasting several hours. There has been no recent intercurrent illness. Sleep has been fragmented since delivery, and caffeine intake has increased modestly; alcohol intake remains minimal. Adherence to prescribed medication is reported as good. No emergency rescue therapy has been required in the last month, but there were two paramedic attendances in August for prolonged confusion without generalised convulsions. No tongue biting or urinary incontinence has been documented. A colleague’s workplace incident report corroborates abrupt onset episodes in bright, high‑noise settings. Neurological examination today is unchanged. Routine bloods last week (U&E, LFTs, FBC) were within reference limits. We have arranged ambulatory EEG with event button and photic stimulation, together with repeat MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) given the change in semiology and tempo. Occupational health advice has been provided regarding avoidance of high‑risk workstations, bright strobe lighting, and unsupervised work at height. The patient has been reminded about DVLA guidance and confirms she is not driving. We discussed strategies to reduce sensory load at work (noise‑attenuating ear protection and glare control) and maintaining a regular sleep pattern where possible. A follow‑up appointment is booked for six weeks, or sooner if further escalation occurs. We will review investigations and consider treatment adjustments once results are available. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Amelia Patel St. Bartholomew’s Hospital Department of Neurology, West Smithfield, London EC1A 7BE Dear Dr Amelia Patel, Emily Carter, DOB: 14-02-1992, Hospital No: H472839 NHS No. 9065123478 12 Brookfield Close, Walthamstow, London E17 5LX Diagnoses: Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification. MRI brain (June 2025) unremarkable. Ambulatory EEG (July 2025) without definitive epileptiform activity. Current Medication: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily Folic acid 5 mg once daily Plan: - Maintain current antiseizure therapy and safety counselling. - Arrange repeat ambulatory EEG with sleep deprivation. - Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D, and Keppra level. - DVLA guidance reinforced: no driving until seizure-free for the legally required period. - Review in clinic in four months or sooner via advice line if further events occur. I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic following multiple recent Emergency Department presentations, with triage notes and nursing documentation reviewed and summarised where relevant. She reports that since giving birth eight months ago, she has noticed a noticeable rise in the number of episodes compared with her pregnancy and pre-pregnancy baseline. The events are described as sudden behavioural arrest with loss of awareness, lasting 1–2 minutes, followed by confusion and fatigue for up to an hour. There is occasionally right-hand twitching and tongue biting; urinary incontinence has not been documented. Her partner’s account during one ED visit corroborated the description of unresponsiveness and brief bilateral shaking. There is no consistent warning, though sleep deprivation and missed meals appear to precede some episodes. ED triage records from August and September 2025 document three attendances with nursing observations of post-event confusion, normal capillary glucose, and no focal neurological deficit on recovery. No clear provoking factors such as infection or intoxicants were identified. ECGs were normal sinus rhythm. CT head (August 2025) was normal. She has been fully compliant with levetiracetam since June 2025; she previously trialled lamotrigine in 2023 but discontinued due to rash. She is currently breastfeeding and reports fragmented sleep. We discussed that disrupted sleep and the demands of the postpartum period can contribute to an increased rate of episodes, and she is arranging additional overnight support where possible. She has a safety plan at home, avoids bathing when alone, and uses a kettle instead of open boiling pans. Seizure first aid has been reviewed with her partner. On examination today she was alert, oriented, and neurologically intact. Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, pulse 76 bpm regular. No signs of systemic illness. In view of the recurrent events, the normal structural imaging, and non-diagnostic ambulatory EEG to date, we will continue levetiracetam at 500 mg twice daily pending further data. If further events occur despite optimising sleep and adherence, we will discuss dose escalation or alternative therapy at the next review once levels and repeat EEG are available. I have provided written information on triggers, medication adherence, and safety, and we have updated her emergency care plan to include rescue midazolam only if generalised convulsive activity persists beyond 5 minutes, to be prescribed after the next review if indicated. I will write again after investigations are completed. Please contact me if there are any concerns in the interim. With best wishes,

Following the introduction of structured night-time childcare support, her sleep has become consolidated and she reports a steady improvement in overall stability. Prior to this change, the reported event frequency was qod (every other week). Over the last several months she describes a complete absence of further episodes, and her day-to-day functioning has normalized. In line with this, neurological examination today is unremarkable. At present she remains episode-free on her current routine without antiseizure medication, with maintained sleep regularity since night-time support began. She understands common red flags (e.g., witnessed loss of awareness with tonic–clonic movements, tongue biting, prolonged post-event confusion) and agrees to seek reassessment should these arise. She also reports reduced daytime fatigue and improved concentration since sleep improved. No further tests are planned at this time. If new features emerge suggestive of epileptic seizures, we would be happy to expedite review. Otherwise, I propose discharge back to your care with open access to our clinic for any future concerns. We will not schedule a routine follow-up, but we remain available should her situation change. Yours sincerely

He reports brief myoclonic jerks on some mornings, particularly with sleep curtailment, and intermittent absence episodes noted by colleagues as brief lapses in conversation. Of particular concern, he and his partner describe clustering of generalised tonic–clonic seizures. Cluster burden increased since 07/Dec/2023; now weekly, five per cluster. He typically experiences a prodrome of diffuse anxiety and photophobia the evening before, followed by a series of convulsions overnight into the early morning. Postictally he has diffuse myalgia and marked fatigue lasting 24–48 hours. The employer’s occupational health summaries corroborate recurrent short-notice absences after nocturnal seizure nights and document witnessed brief staring spells during daytime meetings. He has a history of generalised epilepsy since late adolescence, previously well controlled for several years. No known focal auras, and no clear lateralising motor features have been observed by his partner. Prior EEGs reportedly showed generalised spike–wave activity; brain MRI was normal by prior account. He denies recent head injury, alcohol excess, or recreational drug use. Sleep restriction and high-intensity screen use late at night appear to be consistent precipitants. There is a family history of seizures in a maternal uncle. Current anti-seizure medication is valproate 1,000 mg twice daily, which he has taken for many years with good prior efficacy and tolerability other than weight gain. He reports full adherence. He does not currently drive and understands DVLA regulations pertaining to seizures. No recent medication changes at work. No features suggestive of dissociative events were described, and there has been no psychosis or prolonged confusion outside the immediate postictal period. On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal language, cranial nerves, coordination, tone and power. No focal neurological deficits were elicited. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. We discussed lifestyle measures including sleep regularity, hydration, and minimising late-evening screen exposure; he is motivated to implement these. I have provided a clinic contact pathway for interim concerns. Occupational health may continue to supply periodic summaries, which remain useful collateral sources for monitoring functional outcomes and attendance patterns. Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there is further information from primary care or occupational health that would assist. Yours sincerely

Shah, Mr Daniel Harper, DOB: 22-09-1991, Hospital No: K8429173 NHS No. 9432015876 Flat 12, 5 Riverside Court, Kingston upon Thames, KT1 1AB Diagnosis: Recurrent unprovoked seizures; classification not established Aetiology: Undetermined; no focal neurological deficit on examination, MRI brain (2024) unremarkable; EEG nonspecific background changes Other Medical Problems: History of migraine without aura, currently intermittent and self-managed with simple analgesia Management Plan: - Medication: Continue Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily as current baseline therapy. Add Levetiracetam 250 mg twice daily for two weeks, then increase to 500 mg twice daily if tolerated. Previously trialled Topiramate (discontinued due to cognitive slowing) and Carbamazepine (stopped due to rash). Avoid Topiramate given migraine history unless benefits outweigh cognitive effects. - Monitoring: Seizure diary shows two cluster days this month; sizes unrecorded. Patient will continue to document dates, any precipitating factors, timing relative to missed doses, and recovery features. - Safety/Driving: Discussed standard safety advice around bathing, heights, and operating machinery. Advised to follow DVLA guidance regarding seizures and driving; patient reports not currently driving. - Investigations: Serum Lamotrigine trough level in 4 weeks after dose stability; U&E, LFTs, FBC at the same time. Consider ambulatory EEG if clusters persist despite titration. - Migraine: Maintain hydration and sleep hygiene; patient reports triggers include skipped meals. No change to acute analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen within standard limits). - Follow-up: Review in clinic in 10–12 weeks, sooner if increased frequency or adverse effects. Patient has contact details for the epilepsy nurse specialist for interim support. This patient attended with their partner and described brief episodes characterised by sudden behavioural arrest and loss of awareness, sometimes with lip smacking and post-event confusion lasting up to 20 minutes, though occasional events are limited to brief staring without clear post-ictal phase. There have also been two nocturnal events noted by the partner with unclear semiology; tongue biting not reported. No consistent trigger identified. Medication adherence has improved with use of a weekly pill organiser. In the context of ongoing episodes and the diary entry that seizure diary shows two cluster days this month; sizes unrecorded, we agreed on cautious introduction of adjunctive Levetiracetam with close monitoring for mood changes. No red flags for status epilepticus reported. I reiterated the importance of prompt emergency assessment if a seizure lasts more than five minutes or clusters do not resolve. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr A. Reynolds South Quays Health Centre 12 Riverside Way Bromley Kent BR2 8HT Dear Dr A. Reynolds Mr Daniel Foster, DOB: 14-05-1958, Hospital No: H739516 NHS No. 8472936501 Flat 3, 21 Mill Lane, Bromley, BR1 2QP Diagnoses/summary: Focal epilepsy with impaired awareness, probable temporal lobe onset; longstanding history with prior EEG showing intermittent left temporal sharp waves; MRI 2015 and 2021 non-lesional Previous medication: Carbamazepine (dizziness, hyponatraemia), Levetiracetam (irritability), Valproate (weight gain; stopped on retirement planning), Lacosamide (partial benefit, cognitive slowing), Clobazam PRN (morning grogginess) Not taken: Topiramate, Zonisamide, Lamotrigine, Perampanel, Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Pregabalin, Rufinamide Comorbidities: Hypertension (well controlled), hypercholesterolaemia; cataract surgery left eye 2023. Non-smoker. Newly retired teacher living alone with a regular routine and reduced social contact. I reviewed Mr Daniel Foster in clinic today. He attended alone and brought his written seizure notes. He describes stereotyped focal events beginning with a rising epigastric sensation and pause in speech, occasionally followed by automatisms and brief confusion; no clear generalised tonic–clonic activity for more than two years. Seizure diary shows 2 cluster days this month; sizes unrecorded. He reports good adherence to medication, no recent intercurrent illness, and regular sleep. He does not drive. He has noticed increased isolation since retirement and wonders whether stress around finances may be a trigger, though he keeps a consistent daily routine. Current medication: - Lacosamide 150 mg twice daily - Amlodipine 5 mg once daily - Atorvastatin 20 mg nocte - Vitamin D 1000 IU daily Examination today was unremarkable. Weight stable; BP 128/74. No focal neurological deficits observed. Recent bloods (GP, last month) normal including sodium and liver function. Plan: - We discussed that he has focal epilepsy and ongoing focal impaired-awareness seizures despite current therapy. We reviewed options including trial of lamotrigine or zonisamide, potential switch to brivaracetam, and non-pharmacological measures (structured seizure diary app, regular hydration, and maintaining sleep routine). He prefers to consider a change after discussing with family. - Safety advice reinforced (showers rather than baths, kettle handling, cooking when rested). He confirms he is not driving and understands DVLA guidance. - Community epilepsy nurse to telephone in 4–6 weeks to review frequency and to support social engagement resources (local epilepsy support group, community adult learning). - If cluster frequency increases or injuries occur, we will revisit adding rescue medication and/or medication change. - Routine follow-up in 4 months, sooner if needed. Thank you for your continued care of Mr Daniel Foster. Please forward any interim results. I am happy to see him earlier should circumstances change. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 03 November 2021 Dr Susan University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Susan, William Harris, DOB: 15-02-1965, Hospital No: H563829 NHS No. 9273645810 10 Meadow Park, London, EC1V 9BT Summary/ Diagnoses: Generalised epilepsy following adolescent onset/previous brief absence episodes evolving to generalised tonic–clonic seizures/has practiced aura recognition strategies and describes personal warning features/sleep-onset insomnia/seasonal allergic rhinitis/non-smoker. Medication: Sodium valproate modified-release 500 mg twice daily. Clobazam 10 mg at night as rescue for clustering (patient-directed protocol). Cetirizine 10 mg once daily as needed for allergic rhinitis. I reviewed William Harris in clinic today. He attended alone and provided a clear account of his current seizure control. He has generalised epilepsy. He reports that he continues to use his previously learned aura recognition strategies. In his own words, his typical warning features are “a rising chest fizz, a brief metallic taste, and a snap of light at the edge of vision,” which usually give him enough time to sit or lie down safely and notify a family member if nearby. He keeps a written and app-based diary and synchronises it with his seizure-detection device. Seizures: Device metrics flag one cluster this week; duration 2 h. He states the cluster followed two consecutive late nights and a missed evening dose. He activated his agreed home plan (rest, hydration, clobazam 10 mg) and there were no injuries or emergency attendances. No other events recorded this month by diary or device. Examination: BP 118/72, pulse 68 regular. Neurological examination normal; no focal deficits. Weight stable. No tremor or ataxia. Investigations: Recent liver function tests (last month) normal. Ammonia not elevated. Valproate level within therapeutic range (62 mg/L). Plan: - Continue sodium valproate MR 500 mg twice daily. - Retain clobazam 10 mg as rescue for clustering; patient understands when to take and when to seek help. - Reinforce adherence and sleep hygiene; patient will use phone prompts linked to his device app to reduce missed doses. - No driving given breakthrough cluster this week; will review eligibility per DVLA guidance at next appointment. - Follow-up in 6 months, sooner if further clusters or injuries occur. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences Clinic Date: 19 November 2016 Dr Priya Menon Consultant Neurologist King's College Hospital Department of Neurosciences, King's College Hospital, London SE5 9RS Dear Dr Priya Menon Consultant Neurologist, Daniel Ward, DOB: 14-03-1986, Hospital No: K742193 NHS No. 9075143321 12 Brookfield Close, London, SE15 3AB Thank you for asking me to review this patient in clinic. He attended with his partner and brought notes from a local peer support group, who have been observing his recent events alongside the family. These collateral observations have been particularly helpful in corroborating the temporal pattern and recovery features reported at home. He describes brief episodes with a sudden halt in conversation or activity, a fixed stare, and purposeless fidgeting with both hands. These episodes may be accompanied by a short vocalisation at onset. According to the patient, his partner, and peers from the support group, the events tend to cluster rather than occur singly. Specifically, they report: Weekly clusters, usually 6 or more events within ~2 h. Between clusters he may have single odd spells of unease and a metallic taste without clear behavioural change. Post-event, he is tired, mildly confused, and complains of a dull frontal headache for up to 30–45 minutes, after which he returns to baseline. There is no consistent nocturnal pattern observed by the household, and no clear diurnal trigger has been identified. He has not sustained tongue biting or injuries. He does not recall the episodes, though he sometimes notices a brief rising epigastric sensation shortly beforehand. Medication history includes prior trials of levetiracetam (stopped for mood irritability) and lamotrigine (ineffective at standard dosing per patient report). He currently takes brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily and sertraline 50 mg once daily prescribed by his GP for low mood. He denies hazardous alcohol use or recreational drugs. Sleep can be irregular due to shift work. The peer group have encouraged a trigger diary; his entries so far are incomplete but suggest that missed meals and sleep deprivation may precede the weekly clustering. He has not yet used a wearable seizure-alert device but is open to it. Examination today was unremarkable with normal speech, cranial nerves, limb power, coordination, and gait. No focal neurological deficits were identified. Routine bloods from last month (FBC, U&E, LFTs, glucose) were reportedly within reference ranges as per the GP summary. He has not yet had prolonged ambulatory EEG or inpatient monitoring. At this stage I am still consolidating the semiology and event pattern and will need further objective data. I have discussed obtaining prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture typical clusters and to clarify the nature of these events. He understands the rationale and is agreeable. I have also suggested continuing the trigger diary, with input from the peer support group to document timing, duration, automatisms, awareness, and recovery for each event in a cluster, along with any potential precipitants (sleep loss, missed meals, stress). We will also request prior imaging from the regional hospital; if unavailable or outdated, a 3T MRI epilepsy protocol would be appropriate. No medication changes were made today. I will update you once monitoring is arranged and we have captured representative events. In the meantime, he and his partner have an agreed safety plan for bathing, cooking, and commuting, and the peer group will continue to provide collateral observations which are proving valuable. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Patel St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology, St Mary's Hospital, London W2 1NY Dear Dr Patel, Daniel Morgan, DOB: 12-05-1991, Hospital No: H384920 NHS No. 9051734621 14 Brookfield Court, London, W10 5QP Medication: Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily; Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. Reports good adherence and no recent missed doses. I reviewed Daniel Morgan in clinic today. Since starting a new job in an open-plan office with strong, intermittently flickering overhead lighting and large digital displays, she reports a clear deterioration in her seizure control. She describes weekly clusters, usually four events within ~2 h, most often occurring mid-afternoon on workdays and temporally associated with exposure to the lighting environment. She also notes increased photic sensitivity and eye discomfort preceding episodes in that setting. Outside of work, events are less frequent. Her semiology suggests combined generalised and focal epilepsy: she reports brief focal aware events with visual aura (luminous specks and a shimmering hemifield) sometimes progressing to behavioural arrest with rightward head deviation, and on three occasions in the last eight weeks she has had generalised tonic–clonic seizures from wakefulness without clear focal warning. There is no recent head injury, sleep deprivation is occasional due to shift pattern changes, and she denies alcohol excess. Witness accounts at work describe eyelid fluttering, transient unresponsiveness, and occasional myoclonic jerks on awakening days after late shifts. Post-ictally she experiences fatigue and headache for several hours. No tongue biting or incontinence reported in the recent focal events; present in two of the three generalised events. Examination today was unremarkable between events. Bloods last month (U&E, LFT, FBC) were within reference ranges. She has not yet had a recent EEG in photic stimulation since the job change; prior EEG two years ago showed generalised spike–wave and independent left temporal sharp waves. MRI brain (2022) was structurally normal. Given the deterioration temporally linked to the new workplace lighting, I have discussed strategies to mitigate photic-provoked events (patient-reported interest in non-prescriptive measures such as screen filters and adjusting monitor refresh rates). We will proceed with an urgent repeat EEG including photic stimulation and hyperventilation, and update an occupational risk assessment. I have not altered her antiepileptic medication today pending EEG, but have advised strict adherence, regular sleep pattern, and to avoid known visual triggers where feasible. We will also obtain trough levetiracetam and lamotrigine levels before the next appointment to ensure therapeutic range. Safety advice reinforced regarding driving regulations and seizure first aid at work; her employer has been provided with generic guidance previously. Plan: - Arrange EEG with photic stimulation within 2–3 weeks. - Check trough AED levels prior to EEG. - If clusters persist at current rate (weekly clusters, usually four events within ~2 h) or EEG supports photic sensitivity, we will consider medication optimisation at review, and explore reasonable workplace adjustments. - Follow-up in 6 weeks, sooner if generalised events recur. Yours sincerely

He reports brief morning myoclonic jerks occurring intermittently, and separate focal impaired-awareness seizures characterised by behavioural arrest, fixed gaze, automatisms of the right hand, and post‑event confusion lasting approximately 20–30 minutes. Potential triggers include poor sleep and missed meals; alcohol intake is modest and stable. There is no recent head injury, intercurrent infection, or new medication.
