Past treatments included sodium valproate (weight gain, discontinued) and lacosamide (dizziness). There is no history of status epilepticus. He does not drive and is aware of DVLA guidance. Occupationally he works part‑time from home and uses a seizure diary app, which corroborates the clustering pattern described above. Neurological examination today was unremarkable between events. Routine bloods from last month (U&Es, LFTs, FBC) were within reference ranges. Plan discussed: I have arranged an ambulatory EEG with video capture to better characterise the focal impaired‑awareness seizures within clusters and to sample for generalised discharges. We will also repeat antiseizure medication levels where applicable and check vitamin D. I provided information on sleep regularisation, hydration, and diary‑based trigger tracking. A rescue plan has been reiterated for prolonged clusters, and his partner feels confident with the agreed thresholds for seeking urgent assistance. Follow‑up will be in 8–10 weeks, sooner if there is any change in pattern or injury. Thank you for your referral and ongoing care. Please let me know if there are specific concerns you wish me to address at the next review. Yours sincerely

We aim to respond within 3–5 working days. For urgent clinical concerns, contact 111 or emergency services as appropriate. - Documents: Clinic letters, care plans, and laboratory requests will be viewable in the App under ‘Messages’ and ‘Documents’. Patients can upload home monitoring notes as attachments prior to appointments if helpful. - Prescriptions: Repeat prescriptions can be requested via the NHS App; choose the nominated pharmacy for collection or delivery. Allow 3 working days. - Reminders: We recommended enabling calendar sync within the App to help manage appointments around childcare. Evening telephone slots can be requested via the App message if needed. Next steps: A follow-up telephone review in 4 months will be arranged via the NHS App. Please contact us through the App if an earlier discussion is required. Yours sincerely

Dose 1000mg twice a day Seizures: The patient has focal epilepsy, with carer-supported communication due to a learning disability. Petit mal occur on a near-daily basis, sometimes dozens in a day, making accurate quantification challenging. Generalised convulsions occur once every 12 months. The carer’s seizure log corroborates frequent brief staring episodes with behavioural arrest and eyelid fluttering, each lasting 5–20 seconds, with rapid recovery and no clear post‑ictal confusion. Triggers reported by the carer include sleep deprivation and missed meals. I reviewed Daniel Harper in person with their carer present for history and seizure logging support. The carer provided a diary covering the past three months, which aligns with the above frequency pattern and notes that clusters of brief absences are more pronounced in the late afternoon. There is no recent head injury, intercurrent illness, or medication non‑adherence reported. No new focal neurological deficits on examination today. We discussed treatment adherence strategies and use of a simplified pictorial medication chart to assist the carer with administration and logging. I have advised continuation of current doses while we obtain an updated EEG (including hyperventilation and photic stimulation) to better characterise the frequent brief events, which are likely focal impaired awareness seizures with rapid generalisation not observed. MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) from March 2023 showed no structural lesion. Plan: - Continue Levetiracetam 1000mg twice daily. - Clobazam 10mg nocte may be used for short cluster periods as previously, not exceeding three consecutive nights without clinician advice. - Arrange routine EEG within 6–8 weeks; consider ambulatory EEG if events remain difficult to capture. - Carer to maintain the current seizure log; we provided a revised template with tick‑box features to aid accuracy. - Telephone review in 8 weeks, face‑to‑face in 4–6 months, or sooner if generalised convulsion recurs earlier than expected. Communication/Support: Due to learning disability, information was delivered using simple language and visual prompts. The carer verbalised understanding of rescue plan and documentation requirements. Yours sincerely

Lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily 2. Clobazam 10 mg at night Present Seizure Frequency: epileptic spasm occur on a near-daily basis, sometimes dozens in a day, making accurate quantification challenging. Generalised convulsions occur once every 11 months Context and Triggers (patient-reported): The patient is a frequent international business traveller with irregular sleep patterns, multiple time zone shifts, and variable meal times. They report that long-haul flights, sleep deprivation, and missed or delayed doses around airport security and meetings are common precipitants. Appointments are often by phone due to travel commitments; today’s review was conducted via telephone while the patient was in transit between time zones. Plan of Action: - Maintain lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily to provide baseline coverage for both focal and generalised seizure types. - Optimise clobazam dosing for spasms: increase to 10 mg in the morning and 10 mg at night for two weeks, then review tolerability. If daytime sedation is minimal and spasms persist, consider 10 mg in the morning and 15 mg at night thereafter. - Provide a travel dosing strategy: advise carrying a one-week reserve supply split across two bags, use phone alarms anchored to home time for the first 48 hours after long-haul flights, then switch to local time dosing within 2–3 days to minimise missed doses. - Prescribe a rescue plan for prolonged clusters of spasms: buccal midazolam 10 mg as needed for clusters lasting >20 minutes or where functional impairment prevents safe travel, with clear airline/airport documentation provided. - Arrange an MRI brain with epilepsy protocol (if not performed within last 3 years) and a repeat prolonged EEG (ambulatory preferred to capture daily spasms), to further delineate focal features alongside generalised activity. - Occupational guidance: provide a fit note confirming active epilepsy with near-daily spasms; advise avoidance of lone swimming, working at height, and operating heavy machinery; air travel permissible with adherence to the above medication plan and rescue protocol. - Follow-up: telephone clinic in 8 weeks to assess response to clobazam optimisation and review investigation results. Earlier review if escalation in convulsions, increased injury risk, new neurological deficits, or unacceptable sedation. With best wishes

Rahman, Emily Carter, DOB: 22-11-1991, Hospital No: H392615 NHS No. 8472035196 Flat 3, 9 Rowan Court, Bristol, BS6 7JP Focal Epilepsy Medication: Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily; Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily (patient-reported adherence confirmed via pillbox checks) Lamotrigine Blood Level: 12 September 2025: 4.8 mg/L (laboratory therapeutic reference 1.0–15.0 mg/L). Dose at sampling: 100 mg twice daily; trough level. Seizures: The patient has focal epilepsy. As per diary review and today’s history, focal epileptic spasm occur several times each week, particularly in the evenings. Generalised convulsions seizures are rare, typically four events per year. She notes a prodromal phase of low mood and irritability before some evening events and has been tracking this in a paper diary and mobile calendar; the prodrome is absent before most rare generalised events. I conducted a face-to-face review today. She described brief, stereotyped focal spasms of the left shoulder and neck with awareness retained, often clustering around 8–10 pm, lasting seconds, occasionally in short runs. No injuries reported. The last generalised convulsion was in July 2025 after missed evening doses during a family trip; recovery was uneventful. Sleep deprivation and emotional stress appear to precipitate the evening spasms. She denies daytime drowsiness or new neurological symptoms. Menstrual pattern does not correlate clearly with events. We reviewed her diary entries for the past three months, which show prodromal mood change and irritability beginning 1–3 hours prior to approximately half of the evening focal spasms. She finds that taking quiet time and reducing screen exposure may lessen the intensity but not frequency. She prefers to continue current doses for now while we gather more structured data on triggers. Plan discussed today (patient-reported preferences recorded): - Continue Lamotrigine 100 mg twice daily and Levetiracetam 750 mg twice daily without changes at present. - Continue diary tracking, explicitly logging mood ratings (0–10), sleep duration, caffeine/alcohol intake, and timing of focal spasms and any convulsions. - Safety: She avoids baths when alone and uses a shower seat; no driving. She is aware of first aid measures and when to seek emergency help. - Investigations: Arrange repeat lamotrigine trough level and routine bloods in 8 weeks to coincide with next review; no immediate imaging changes requested. - Follow-up: Telephone review in 10 weeks to reassess frequency and prodromal features. Yours sincerely

He reports cumulative fatigue across the week, with perceived worsening of seizure control on late and consecutive shifts. He still has focal impaired awareness seizures two times per day, drop attacks occurring in batches, and tonic-clonic seizures 2 times per month, this long-standing pattern has persisted without major change. However, he feels more drained after each cluster, with slower recovery times and greater post-event confusion when shifts run over or when staffing levels are short. There have been no recent medication changes, no intercurrent illness, and no documented injuries, though he reports near-misses during patient manoeuvres. He has kept partial diaries which suggest clustering on days following interrupted sleep and heavy manual handling. No clear triggers beyond sleep disruption and fatigue are identified. He denies recent alcohol use and reports reliable adherence to prescribed treatment. On review today, neurological examination between events was unchanged. No new focal neurological signs were elicited. We discussed work pattern influences and his impression of deterioration relates primarily to increased recovery time, reduced stamina between events, and increasing anxiety about safety at work, rather than a numerical escalation of seizures. A risk discussion was had around drop attacks during patient transfers. He understands the need to avoid lone handling where feasible and is seeking reasonable adjustments. We agreed he will liaise with his line manager and occupational health regarding shift regularity and rest breaks, and he will continue to maintain a structured seizure and fatigue diary to capture patterns around late shifts. Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure regimen unchanged (patient-reported stable adherence). - Occupational health referral requested by patient to explore regularised breaks, reduced consecutive late shifts, and assistance with heavy transfers where possible. - Seizure and fatigue diaries to be maintained, with emphasis on sleep duration, timing of meals, and manual-handling episodes. - Safety advice reiterated; he will avoid high-risk tasks immediately after any warning symptoms. - Follow-up in 8 weeks, sooner if injuries occur or if recovery periods lengthen further. Yours sincerely,

note_text_single_line: Neurology Clinic Clinic Date: 11 May 2019 Dr Patel Riverside Neurology Service Outpatient Department, Riverside Health Centre, 14 Mill Street, Bristol BS1 4AB Dear Dr Patel, Re: Laura Bennett, DOB: 14-07-1993, Hospital No: H927451, NHS No: 7401928653 Address: Flat 3, 22 Brook Lane, Bristol, BS3 2QZ Thank you for asking me to review Laura Bennett in our neurology clinic today, attended with her mother, who is the primary caregiver. We discussed current symptoms, rescue plans and device checks where relevant. There have been no recent hospital admissions, and no injuries reported. Seizure history and current status: Seizure control is inconsistent and while the caregiver perceives stability, she continues to have nightly generalised convulsions seizures and intermittent tonic seizures four times per year, this has been her enduring seizure profile for many years. The family keeps a calendar record which corroborates this pattern over the last 12 months. There are no identified new triggers; menses and intercurrent illness can still exacerbate events. No episodes of status epilepticus were reported. Post-ictal recovery remains slow but predictable, with fatigue and transient confusion. Medications and adherence: - No recent changes to regular anti-seizure medicines per caregiver report. - Rescue plan remains available; no rescue treatment used in the past three months. - Adherence is reported as good; no adverse effects volunteered beyond mild daytime sleepiness. Investigations and observations today: - Neurological examination: unchanged from prior notes; no new focal deficits. - Bloods and drug levels were not repeated today; last routine profile three months ago reportedly unremarkable per GP correspondence. - No new imaging since last review; family did not report interval events warranting urgent re-imaging. Care plan discussed: - Continue current management pathway as tolerated, with emphasis on safety measures at night and consistent record-keeping. - We reviewed seizure first aid and when to seek emergency help; the caregiver demonstrated good understanding. - Community epilepsy nurse contact details were re-confirmed for ongoing support. Follow-up: We agreed to review Laura Bennett in six months, or sooner if there is an increase in frequency, clusters, injuries, or any change in the established pattern described above. Yours sincerely,

Patel, Emily Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: E927451 NHS No. 6045812379 Flat 2, 16 Rowan Close, Eastborough EB3 1QP Diagnoses: Adult-onset seizure disorder; history of childhood febrile seizures noted. Current Medication: - Levetiracetam 1 g bd - Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent use for clusters) Plan: - Continue current antiseizure regimen without changes today while we complete further evaluation. - Arrange prolonged ambulatory EEG and MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to clarify seizure onset and aid risk stratification. - Provide seizure first-aid and nocturnal supervision advice; reinforce SUDEP risk discussion given ongoing nocturnal events. - Safety counselling: bathing supervision, avoid heights/open water; driving not permitted and DVLA guidance reviewed. - Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if escalation occurs; consider medication optimisation or addition depending on results and tolerability. I reviewed Emily Carter in clinic today with her partner present. She reports a long-standing history of childhood febrile seizures, with no clear events through adolescence. In adulthood she developed recurrent seizures. Seizure control is inconsistent and while the caregiver perceives stability, she continues to have nightly generalised tonic-clonic seizures and intermittent tonic seizures 2 - 3 times per year, this has been her enduring seizure profile for many years. She describes the nocturnal events as occurring during sleep with a bitten tongue on several occasions and morning headache and myalgia. Daytime events are rare. There are no clear catamenial patterns. She identifies sleep deprivation and intercurrent illness as potential precipitants. She is adherent with her current medication. Previous trials of lamotrigine were discontinued due to rash; topiramate caused cognitive side effects. No recent injuries, but there have been two prior bed falls without major harm. There is no family history of adult seizures. Neurological examination today is unremarkable. Routine blood tests earlier this month were within reference limits. We discussed lifestyle measures, nocturnal safeguards (monitoring device, side-lying positioning), and the importance of regular sleep. An updated seizure diary was provided. I will review her after investigations to consider adjustments such as clobazam regularisation at night or alternative adjuncts depending on tolerability and findings. With best wishes, Yours sincerely

With best wishes,

note_text_single_line: St Mary's Hospital Institute of Neurology Clinic Date: 14 October 2025 Dr Hannah McKenzie Greenford Road Medical Practice 214 Greenford Road, London, UB6 8QN Dear Dr Hannah McKenzie, Sophie Bennett, DOB: 12-03-1991, Hospital No: H482930 NHS No. 9073615248 Flat 3, 29 Larkspur Court, London, W5 4TA Reason for review: Follow-up after recent long-haul travel with reported sleep disruption, jet lag, and perceived worsening of events. History since last clinic: Following cross-time-zone travel to visit family, she reports 10–14 days of circadian disruption with fragmented sleep and heightened anxiety about further events. She describes increased morning myoclonic twitches and more frequent brief lapses in attention during the first fortnight after return. She has also noted headaches and irritability when sleep debt accumulates. No injuries, tongue biting, or incontinence reported. She maintains good medication adherence (no missed doses reported) and denies intercurrent illness or alcohol excess. A family member has begun keeping a simple diary of events and sleep duration. Seizure description and frequency: There has been little alteration in seizure frequency over the past year; she experiences one to two generalised tonic-clonic seizures yearly with the longest seizure-free period being three weeks. She has three - four absences per day. In addition, she suffers clusters of myoclonic jerks and occasional tonic seizures, these occur roughly once a month. No seizures have been recorded since her last appointment. Despite the above baseline, she perceives deterioration in the days following the flight, particularly with early morning jerks and daytime lapses, coinciding with reduced total sleep and shifting sleep–wake times. She feels overall confidence has worsened and is avoiding public transport as a precaution. Examination: Neurological examination today is non-focal. Cardiovascular observations are within normal limits. No injuries or post-ictal features. Investigations: - Recent bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) from GP two weeks ago were within reference ranges per patient report; we have requested the results for confirmation. - No recent EEG or MRI since prior review; we will consider repeat studies if functional impact continues despite sleep regularisation. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily. - Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily. No notable adverse effects except intermittent insomnia around travel. She uses melatonin 2 mg prolonged-release intermittently, patient-initiated, with partial benefit. Management plan discussed with patient: - Emphasised regular sleep–wake routine, particularly in the 10–14 days following long-haul flights; she will continue a sleep diary alongside the seizure diary kept by her relative. - Agreed to trial timed light exposure in the mornings and avoidance of late-evening screens for two hours before bed as patient-led measures. - We discussed that if perceived daytime lapses continue beyond the next month despite improved sleep, we may consider a small up-titration of levetiracetam or addition of a morning-release melatonin regimen; she prefers to defer medication changes today. - Safety advice reinforced regarding bathing/showering and use of public transport at less busy times while confidence is low; she understands when to seek emergency help. - We will review in three months, sooner if events escalate or if any generalised convulsive event occurs. Summary: Although no events have been documented since the last appointment, she reports a deterioration in perceived control and daily function following cross-time-zone travel, in the context of circadian disruption. Objective frequency over the past year remains as above. We will prioritise stabilising sleep and closely monitor the impact on daytime function before altering treatment. Yours sincerely,

I reviewed Sophie Williams in clinic today accompanied by her partner. She has been practising aura recognition strategies as previously discussed and was able to describe her typical warnings in her own words. She reports a rising epigastric sensation, a metallic taste, and a brief sense of detachment lasting 10–20 seconds, which she identifies as her focal aware phase. She has been using these early symptoms to alert others and to move to a safe position, which she feels has reduced injury risk. We discussed ongoing self-management with particular emphasis on prompt response to auras, maintaining regular sleep and meals, and continuing the diary. She is aware of SUDEP information and first aid measures. We agreed to continue current management and to monitor for any evolution of her focal symptoms or change in seizure semiology. She will contact the service sooner if she notes prolonged clusters, injuries, or any adverse effects from medication. Plan: - Continue current anti-seizure therapy as tolerated. - Persist with aura recognition strategies and safety planning as practised. - Maintain seizure diary including potential triggers, duration, and recovery. - Routine follow-up in 4 months, or earlier if clinical change occurs. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Department of Neurology Clinic Date: 02 October 2025 Dr Emily Hart St George’s University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Department of Neurology, Blackshaw Road, London SW17 0QT Dear Dr Emily Hart, Michael Carter, DOB: 14-03-1991, Hospital No: H392847 NHS No. 9012745632 Flat 5, 28 Clapham Park Road, London SW4 7BN Diagnoses: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (both generalised and focal seizure types) with emerging new event phenotype. MRI brain (2017) non-lesional. EEG (2023) mixed findings with intermittent generalised spike-wave and independent left temporal sharp waves. Current Medication: Levetiracetam 1 g bd Lamotrigine 150 mg bd Clobazam 10 mg nocte (intermittent daytime 5 mg as rescue on high-risk days by patient report) Plan: - Urgent ambulatory EEG with video capture to characterise new events and correlate with diary. - Increase Lamotrigine to 175 mg bd (subject to tolerability and bloods) and consider rationalisation of clobazam depending on EEG correlation. - Safety counselling reinforced regarding bathing, heights, cooking, and SUDEP risk; car driving remains contraindicated. - Bloods today: FBC, U&E, LFT, bone profile, vitamin D; check antiepileptic levels where applicable. - Refer to epilepsy specialist nurse for rescue plan review and to falls clinic re daily drop attacks. - Consider surgical workup if focal onset to generalisation is confirmed (repeat MRI with epilepsy protocol and MDT discussion). - Review in clinic in 8–10 weeks; earlier if events escalate or injuries occur. I reviewed Michael Carter in my clinic today following concerns about a deterioration in his epilepsy, specifically the emergence of a new event phenotype compared with his prior descriptions. He described episodes over the past three months featuring abrupt behavioural arrest with bilateral arm stiffening and a forward lurch, sometimes preceded by a brief rising epigastric sensation and followed by several minutes of confusion; these differ from his usual focal impaired-awareness spells and his established generalised tonic-clonic seizures. His partner has captured two events on a smartphone video, which suggest sudden atonic elements with potential focal evolution; we will seek objective characterisation with ambulatory EEG and video correlation. Seizure frequency remains unchanged over the last six months; he continues to have up to 3 generalised tonic-clonic seizures per year, rarely achieving more than ten consecutive seizure-free days. He also has daily drop attacks. Furthermore, focal impaired-awareness seizures with disorientation are reported every four to six weeks. No events have occurred since his most recent review. While the overall count is stable, the qualitative change in semiology and the daily drop attacks indicate functional deterioration and increased risk of injury. He reports two minor head impacts in the kitchen without loss of consciousness and increased postictal fatigue. Sleep is fragmented by early-morning awakenings; alcohol intake is minimal; adherence is good by his account and blister-pack records. His background is of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, with both generalised and focal seizure types documented historically. Prior EEGs have shown generalised spike-wave discharges as well as left temporal sharp waves, and his MRI has been non-lesional. We discussed that the appearance of new atonic-like events may represent evolution of his epilepsy or medication-related lowering of threshold for drop attacks, though the latter is less likely given stable dosing. Given the injury risk, I recommend proceeding with ambulatory EEG urgently and modestly up-titrating lamotrigine while monitoring for rash, dizziness, or diplopia. If the new events are confirmed as focal onset with rapid generalisation or as true atonic seizures, we will revisit broad treatment options including optimisation of current regimen, considering sodium channel agent substitution, or referral for surgical/neuromodulation evaluation (VNS/DBS) after MDT discussion. I have reinforced safety precautions and provided written information on seizure first aid. The epilepsy specialist nurse will update his rescue plan and explore protective headwear for high-risk activities. I will write with results and see him back in 8–10 weeks, sooner if there is any further deterioration or significant injury. With best wishes,

He and his employer have noted that his events cluster on shifts in the brightly lit packing zones, particularly after prolonged exposure. He reports increased anxiety about attending work and has begun to avoid certain aisles; his supervisor has documented multiple near-falls on site. She also reports greater post-ictal confusion and headache compared to prior baseline. There have been no injuries, but she has required assistance at work on two occasions due to prolonged recovery. She remains fully adherent to lamotrigine and levetiracetam and denies missed doses. No intercurrent illness or alcohol excess. Menses are regular and there is no clear catamenial pattern. She has been undertaking longer shifts, and sleep has been reduced to approximately 5–6 hours on several weekdays, which may be contributory. There is no new medication or supplement use. Examination in clinic today was non-focal and unchanged. Routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs) from last month were within normal limits per patient report; we have requested copies for our records. She has not yet undergone the repeat EEG we previously suggested; we have re-booked this to evaluate for any evolution in interictal generalised spike–wave activity. Given the altered aura phenomenology with more rapid evolution, we regard this as a deterioration in her condition despite the apparent stability of event counts. We discussed lifestyle regularisation, seizure first aid, and maintaining a seizure diary with specific attention to aura onset, duration, and precipitating factors. She is fit to continue current duties with caution and agreed workplace adjustments around rest breaks. Driving status was reviewed in accordance with DVLA guidance; she understands her obligations to report and to cease driving if criteria are not met. Plan: • Continue lamotrigine 150 mg AM / 200 mg PM and levetiracetam 1000 mg BD unchanged for now while we reassess. • Arrange early EEG and consider ambulatory recording if routine study is non-diagnostic. • Repeat serum lamotrigine level for reference (non-urgent). • Follow-up in the neurology clinic in 8–10 weeks or sooner if escalation occurs (e.g., injuries, clustering, or prolonged post-ictal states). We will keep you updated following investigations. Yours sincerely

He describes increased post-ictal fatigue, prolonged recovery times after convulsive seizures, and more pronounced cognitive fog affecting study and work performance. He attended unaccompanied and was able to give a clear account of his history. He describes two distinct seizure types consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The focal events begin with a rising epigastric sensation and a brief pause with loss of awareness, during which he is noted to stare and fumble with nearby objects for up to 60–90 seconds, followed by several minutes of confusion. Separately, he has generalised tonic–clonic seizures that typically occur from sleep or in the early morning without a clear prodrome. There is no consistent trigger identified, though he reports that missed meals and fragmented sleep have occasionally preceded events. Following introduction of lamotrigine, there has been a clear improvement in control, with just nine generalised tonic-clonic seizures documented this year to date. He also reports a reduction in the frequency of focal impaired-awareness episodes, now occurring roughly once every three to four weeks, usually clustering after periods of stress or disrupted sleep. He keeps a written seizure diary, which correlates with this history. There is no history of status epilepticus. Post-ictally he experiences myalgia and headache for several hours, but there is no prolonged confusion beyond the immediate recovery period. He denies tongue-biting outside of the generalised events and has had two minor falls this year without injury. There is no current use of alcohol or recreational drugs, and he remains independent with activities of daily living. He has limited social contact but is open to community support should it be available. Current anti-seizure medication is lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, well tolerated without rash, dizziness, or diplopia. He is not on any other anti-seizure therapy at present, and there have been no recent medication changes. He is adherent and uses a pill organiser. Sleep hygiene is reasonable; he typically retires at 22:30 and rises at 06:30. On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal language, intact cranial nerves, normal tone and power throughout, symmetrical reflexes, and a normal gait. There were no focal neurological deficits detected. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. In summary, the clinical picture is of combined generalised and focal epilepsy, with both focal impaired-awareness seizures and separate generalised tonic–clonic seizures. Seizure control has improved on lamotrigine, with a clear reduction in generalised events this year as above. note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 29 December 2021 Dr Priya Menon Riverside Medical Practice 12 Wharf Street, London, SE8 3AB Dear Dr Priya Menon Andrew Collins, DOB: 21-11-1982, Hospital No: H392774 NHS No. 7483926150 Flat 4, 28 Millbank Court, London, SE1 7QP I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. Since our last contact he has been using a seizure diary app to log symptoms, rescue medication usage, and potential triggers. He reports generally feeling well and has been attending work full-time. Sleep has been variable due to shift patterns, and he has noted higher stress levels around project deadlines. He denies recent alcohol binges and has maintained hydration and meals as advised. He mentioned occasional brief startles in the mornings over the past few weeks, which he recorded as isolated jerks with no confusion. Regarding recent events, his seizure diary confirms the following: He did not have seizures for over 6 months, but then reported two generalised tonic-clonic seizures two Fridays ago, each preceded by myoclonic jerks. He described the jerks as brief, occurring in clusters over a few minutes before each convulsion. On both occasions the events occurred shortly after waking. The app entries include witness notes from his partner describing bilateral stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking lasting approximately 90–120 seconds, with a post-ictal phase of about 30 minutes. No injuries were recorded; there was tongue biting on the second event but no incontinence. He did not require emergency services and recovered at home. Medication adherence is self-reported as high and corroborated by his app’s reminder logs. He remains on Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d., Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d., and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He reports mild daytime fatigue and intermittent irritability, which he attributes to work stress; no rash, visual disturbance, or gait issues. He uses a smartwatch linked to the diary for sleep tracking; data around the seizure dates indicate reduced sleep duration and increased sleep fragmentation. He has logged caffeine intake on the preceding days as higher than usual. Neurological examination today is unremarkable. Vital signs are stable. No focal deficits. We reviewed his safety measures: he continues to avoid heights, swims only with supervision, and has updated his workplace seizure action plan. He is aware of DVLA guidance and has paused driving; we discussed ongoing compliance with statutory requirements. Plan: I have requested an updated set of routine bloods (including U&E, LFTs, FBC) and a drug level for Lamotrigine to assist with future decision-making. I have also scheduled an EEG within the next 4–6 weeks to capture any interictal changes, and we will review his sleep routine and diary trends at that time. He will continue current medications unchanged for now, and we agreed on close monitoring via the app with prompts to flag any further convulsions, clusters of myoclonic jerks, or injuries. We discussed stress management techniques and regular sleep-wake timing; he is amenable to trialling app-based sleep hygiene prompts. No immediate changes to treatment were made today. I will review him again in three months or sooner if there is any recurrence or escalation in events. Please feel free to contact me if you require further information. Yours sincerely

Management Plan: - Continue current VNS settings as per last optimisation; patient and carer trained in magnet use and report reduced need for activation since the last review. - Maintain current anti-seizure medication regimen unchanged, as per stability over several years. - Routine bloods for general health monitoring via GP: FBC, U&Es, LFTs and thyroid profile in 6 months. - Annual VNS device interrogation and battery longevity check at our device clinic; earlier review if there is any change in seizure pattern or VNS-related discomfort. - Safety and lifestyle: patient reports improved alertness and has gradually increased community activities; continue standard seizure first aid education for carers though no recent use required. - Follow-up in 9–12 months, sooner if breakthrough events occur or if any adverse effects emerge. Since VNS optimisation at her previous appointment, the patient and her mother report sustained improvements in alertness, sleep regularity and day-to-day confidence. There have been no emergency presentations, no injuries, and no episodes suggestive of nocturnal events. Appetite and weight remain stable, and there are no concerns regarding mood or behaviour. Examination today is unremarkable; the VNS generator site is well-healed with no tenderness, and device cycling is comfortable. Given the excellent stability, we will maintain the current plan and continue to monitor device parameters at scheduled intervals. Yours sincerely

Valproate modified‑release 750 mg twice daily 2. Clobazam 10 mg at night 3. Rescue: Buccal midazolam 10 mg as per community protocol (not used in the last two years) Present Seizure Frequency: With a history of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, previously experiencing tonic seizures, atonic drop attacks and atypical absences, she has now been seizure free for one and a half years. Background and Occupational Context: She works full‑time in gardening/groundskeeping, mainly outdoors. She reports seasonal variation in workload with prolonged exertion during summer months and occasional heat exposure. She remains meticulous with hydration and medication timing, and uses a phone reminder for her evening dose when overtime is required. No episodes of presyncope, injuries, or missed doses reported. Sleep averages 7–8 hours and caffeine intake is moderate. Plan of Action: - Continue current anti‑seizure regimen (valproate MR 750 mg twice daily and clobazam 10 mg at night) given sustained seizure freedom and good tolerability. - Occupational advice (patient‑reported understanding and agreed): maintain regular dosing schedules during peak summer shifts; carry water and electrolytes; schedule brief shaded rest breaks to mitigate heat stress; avoid lone working on laddered pruning; and continue to wear head protection when using powered equipment. - Monitoring: arrange annual bloods (FBC, LFTs, U&E) and valproate level prior to morning dose in 3 months to coincide with routine occupational health review. - Rescue plan: retain buccal midazolam in first‑aid kit at depot; colleagues aware of protocol though not required in the last two years. - Follow‑up: review in 9–12 months or earlier if breakthrough events, medication side effects, or changes in work pattern (e.g., extended heat exposure) occur. With best wishes

With a history of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, previously experiencing tonic seizures, atonic drop attacks and atypical absences, she has now been seizure free for several years. Co-existing migraine without aura. Neuroimaging/EEG: MRI brain 2018 and 2024 unremarkable for structural epileptogenic lesion. Historical EEGs showed generalised slow spike–wave in childhood; most recent routine EEG (2023) normal background with no interictal epileptiform discharges. Current medication: Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; Topiramate 50 mg nightly (for migraine prophylaxis); Folic acid 5 mg daily; Vitamin D3 1000 IU daily. Not previously tolerated/ceased: Levetiracetam (mood irritability), Valproate (weight gain, discontinued when planning family), Carbamazepine (dizziness), Clobazam PRN previously (no longer required). Allergies: No known drug allergies. Interval history: I reviewed Wendy in clinic today; she attended alone and brought her seizure diary. She works in a distribution warehouse and reports that since the peak season ended, overtime and workload have reduced significantly. She links this reduction in fatigue and irregular hours with better overall control and wellbeing. Sleep has improved to 7–8 hours nightly; she has resumed light exercise. With a history of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, previously experiencing tonic seizures, atonic drop attacks and atypical absences, she has now been seizure free for several years, and in the past 12 months has had no events suggestive of focal aware or impaired awareness seizures. She denies auras, drop attacks, or nocturnal events. No injuries or hospital attendances. Adverse effects/functional status: No cognitive slowing on current regimen; mood stable; weight stable; no diplopia or ataxia. Migraines have reduced from 4/month to approximately 1/month since starting low-dose topiramate; uses simple analgesia sparingly. Lifestyle/safety: Adheres to DVLA guidance and remains eligible to drive given sustained seizure freedom. Avoids sleep deprivation and excessive caffeine. No alcohol misuse. Reports good medication adherence with phone reminders. Plan: - Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily unchanged. - Continue topiramate 50 mg nightly for migraine prophylaxis; no change today. - Routine bloods via GP: FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D over next 6–8 weeks for general monitoring. - Encourage ongoing sleep hygiene and regular routine at work; written information provided on seizure first aid for her employer, though not recently required. - Follow-up: routine review in 9–12 months, earlier if any breakthrough events, red flags, pregnancy planning, or adverse effects. Thank you for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there are any concerns in the interim. Yours sincerely

Rahman Thomas Green, DOB: 09-02-1991, Hospital No: H927461 NHS No. 7452019863 Flat 3, 12 Millbank Court, Bromley, BR1 4JP Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient describes both generalised tonic–clonic seizures and focal impaired-awareness events), seizure pattern exacerbated by circadian disruption from rotating night shifts MRI brain 2018 reported structurally normal brain; routine EEG 2018 showed intermittent generalised spike–wave with occasional left temporal sharp transients; sleep-deprived EEG 2021 with generalised polyspike–wave and rare left temporal spikes, consistent with combined generalised and focal epileptiform activity Previous medication: Valproate (effective for generalised seizures but stopped due to weight gain and tremor), Carbamazepine (worsened generalised discharges), Levetiracetam (behavioural irritability), Lamotrigine (partial benefit), Clobazam PRN (helpful for clusters but sedation), Topiramate (word-finding difficulty), Zonisamide (insomnia), Lacosamide (limited benefit), Perampanel (mood effects) Not taken: Brivaracetam, Cenobamate, Rufinamide, Ethosuximide, Pregabalin, Tiagabine Other background: Shift-based employment including nights; longstanding irregular sleep; no history of significant head injury; no family history of epilepsy; does not drive I reviewed Thomas Green in clinic today. He also describes occasional early-morning generalised seizures after consecutive night shifts. Post-ictally he is fatigued with myalgia and mild confusion for several hours. Current medication: - Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily - Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily - Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used approximately twice monthly) Adverse effects: reports irritability on levetiracetam mitigated somewhat with dose timing and exercise; otherwise tolerating regimen. Blood pressure 122/76. Investigations: U&Es, LFTs, FBC from August 2025 normal; Vitamin D borderline low (51 nmol/L). No evidence of hyponatraemia. ECG last year normal sinus rhythm. Discussion/Plan: - We discussed that his pattern and investigations support a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. We reviewed the role of sleep and circadian stability; he is a rotating shift worker including nights and feels the night-to-day swing is the principal precipitant of clusters. - Medication: continue Lamotrigine 150 mg BD. Reduce Levetiracetam to 750 mg BD trial if mood symptoms persist after we implement sleep measures; if seizures worsen, revert to 1 g BD. Consider Brivaracetam as a future alternative if irritability remains problematic. Continue Clobazam 10 mg nocte PRN at onset of cluster for up to 3 nights; he understands the sedation risk. - Rescue/cluster plan: maintain diary; if three or more focal events occur in 24 hours, he will take Clobazam that night and prioritise sleep recovery. He has agreed to call the epilepsy nurse line if clusters persist beyond 48 hours or any injury occurs. - Occupational guidance: provided a written note supporting trial of forward-rotating shifts and at least two consecutive recovery sleep periods after nights; he will discuss with his employer’s occupational health team. We covered safety at work and at home (showers rather than baths, avoid heights/ladders alone, caution with machinery when sleep-deprived). - Driving: not driving currently; we reiterated DVLA regulations and the need to inform DVLA if applicable. - Lifestyle: advised consistent sleep window on off-duty days, morning light exposure after night shifts, and limiting caffeine after midday. Vitamin D supplementation 1000 IU daily suggested given borderline level (over the counter acceptable). - Further investigations: none urgently required. If control remains suboptimal after schedule adjustments, we will discuss ambulatory EEG to better characterise sleep-related triggers and consider Brivaracetam or Cenobamate depending on response and tolerability. Follow-up: Epilepsy nurse telephone follow-up in 6 weeks to review shift adjustments, mood, and cluster frequency; clinic review in 4 months or earlier if clusters increase in frequency or if he has any generalised seizures despite improved sleep strategy. Please do not hesitate to contact me if further information is required. Thank you for your ongoing care. Yours sincerely

Triggers are not clearly defined, though she suspects sleep disruption and high-stress days may lower her threshold. Night-time events are rare by her account; the partner has witnessed two nocturnal episodes over the past six months, each with brief confusion on waking. Regarding frequency, the current pattern is variable but with a recognisable cadence. She can occasionally manage five days without seizures, though this is usually followed by a day of clustering, with two to four events. This pattern is corroborated by diary entries and partner observation and is consistent with peer notes taken during two observed days earlier this summer. Rescue measures have not been required to date, and there have been no emergency attendances in the last twelve months. Medication history includes levetiracetam previously (discontinued due to mood irritability), lamotrigine (partial benefit but dose-limited by rash), and currently lacosamide at a moderate dose, which she tolerates. We also discussed general measures: consistent sleep routine, hydration, and pacing on high-demand days; she will continue these self-management strategies. I will update you once monitoring is complete and we have a clearer synthesis. Please let me know if there are interim concerns or if new information arises from your records. Yours sincerely

There is no recent intercurrent illness, alcohol excess, or new medications. She denies missed anti‑seizure medication, though acknowledges variable timing on late shifts. Menses regular; no pregnancy. Current treatment: lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily; levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. note_text_single_line: KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE Clinic Date: 31 October 2021 Dr Anita Desai Riverside Community Health Centre 12 Riverside Way, Southwark, London SE1 5HT Dear Dr Anita Desai Mr Michael Turner, DOB: 14-03-1987, Hospital No: H738291 NHS No. 9430021187 Room 4, Willow House, 3 Hartwell Street, London SE15 2QF I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. He attended alone and reports ongoing difficulties associated with recent housing instability. He is currently awaiting relocation from temporary accommodation; crowded living conditions have been noted and he feels this is disrupting sleep and routine. He remains engaged with his medication regimen and brings a diary of events. Seizure pattern has remained largely unchanged since the last clinic visit. He suffers clusters of absence seizures on four to five days each week. Nocturnal tonic seizures continue to occur around once per year. No daytime convulsions have been recorded recently. He reports brief post-event fatigue after clusters, but no new injuries, tongue biting, or prolonged post-ictal confusion. There have been no emergency attendances since the previous review. Current medications as recorded today: Levetiracetam 1500 mg b.d.; Sodium Valproate 500 mg t.d.s.; Lamotrigine 100 mg b.d.; and Clobazam 10 mg nocte. He remains adherent and uses a pill organiser. He describes intermittent daytime tiredness that he attributes partly to broken sleep in the current living situation. No rash, mood deterioration, or gastrointestinal upset reported. Weight and basic observations today are unremarkable. We discussed potential seizure triggers. He notes irregular sleep, increased ambient noise at night, and stress linked to the impending move. He has reduced caffeine and is attempting more consistent sleep times where feasible. He continues not to drive and understands DVLA guidance. Given the stability of the overall pattern and the imminent change in living circumstances, we agreed not to alter medication today. He will continue the current regimen, maintain the seizure diary, and we will reassess following relocation, when sleep and routines may be more settled. I have provided written advice on sleep hygiene and signposted him to local support services for housing-related stress. He is aware to contact the service or attend A&E if events change in character, become prolonged, or if new daytime convulsions occur. Plan: - Continue current antiepileptic regimen unchanged. - Maintain detailed seizure and trigger diary. - Reinforce sleep hygiene; continue avoidance of sleep deprivation where possible. - Community epilepsy nursing team to check in within 4 weeks. - Review in clinic in 3 months, or sooner if there is any deterioration or change in event semiology. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery Clinic Date: 02 February 2020 Dr Susan University College Hospital National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, Queen Square, London WC1N 3BG Dear Dr Susan, William Harris, DOB: 15-02-1965, Hospital No: H563829 NHS No. 9273645810 10 Meadow Park, London, EC1V 9BT Summary/Diagnoses: Focal epilepsy following prior traumatic brain injury; persistent cognitive impairment; osteoporosis; past alcohol dependence with alcoholic hepatitis; currently residing in supported accommodation; smoker; reports social alcohol use and is actively reducing intake. Medication: - Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily - Tegretol Retard (carbamazepine) 400 mg twice daily - Topiramate 75 mg morning and 100 mg evening - Vitamin B compound, Calcichew, Strontium sachets, Thiamine, Atorvastatin, Lansoprazole, Bisoprolol, Ramipril, Carbocisteine, Aqueous cream I reviewed Bill in clinic today, accompanied by his key worker, who has supported him for the past year. He reports improved sleep routine and better adherence to morning medications with use of a blister pack. He is engaging in light physiotherapy for balance and right-sided stiffness; gait is slow but he mobilises independently with a single-point stick. There have been no recent falls. Appetite is stable and weight is unchanged. He acknowledges occasional social alcohol use at family events but states he is reducing and aiming for abstinence; no binges have been reported by staff. Epilepsy history and current status: Bill has focal epilepsy. Seizure pattern has remained largely unchanged since the last clinic visit. He suffers clusters of absence seizures on five days each month. Nocturnal tonic seizures continue to occur around once per year. No daytime convulsions have been recorded recently. He and staff are keeping a simple monthly seizure diary, which aligns with the above pattern. Known triggers include missed morning doses and sleep loss; neither has occurred in the past two months according to care records. No injuries from seizures have been reported. Examination: Alert and oriented to person and place; mild executive dysfunction on conversational testing. Speech fluent. Cranial nerves intact. Tone mildly increased in right leg with reduced right ankle dorsiflexion; power otherwise antigravity throughout. Sensation grossly intact to light touch. Gait slow with reduced right foot clearance; no ataxia. Cardiovascular and respiratory exams unremarkable. Investigations: No new imaging since prior MRI showing left frontal gliosis consistent with old traumatic change. Routine bloods from GP two months ago reportedly normal including LFTs, U&Es, and vitamin D; we will request results for our records. No adverse haematological effects reported on current antiseizure regimen. Plan: - Continue current antiseizure medications unchanged given stable focal epilepsy pattern. - Reinforce adherence and sleep hygiene; continue seizure diary. - Request recent blood results from practice (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D); repeat locally if unavailable. - Physiotherapy to continue for gait and right leg stiffness; encourage daily walking within supported setting. - Support ongoing reduction in social alcohol use; no medication changes on this basis today. - Follow-up in 6 months, sooner if seizure pattern worsens or daytime convulsions occur. Yours sincerely

note_text_single_line: Epilepsy Centre Neurosciences Division From: Dr Emma Shah (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Sent: 19 November 2023 10:15 To: epilepsy.centre@nhs.net Cc: Dr Michael Byrne (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST); Dr Priya Nair (KING'S COLLEGE HOSPITAL NHS FOUNDATION TRUST) Subject: Deterioration during exam period and medication adjustment Hi Emma Epilepsy Diagnosis: Type not classified at present pending further evaluation Present Medication: 1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily 2. Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily 3. Rescue: Buccal midazolam 10 mg as needed for clusters (not used in the past six months) Present Seizure Frequency: Her parents report a reduction in convulsive events, with only a single tonic-clonic seizure over the past six months. Brief myoclonic jerks persist daily on awakening but are considered tolerable. There have been no prolonged or status episodes since treatment escalation. Context and Current Concerns: Despite the above, her overall condition is deteriorating functionally during the current exam/professional assessment season. She and her parents describe marked escalation in stress, poor sleep continuity, early morning awakenings, and increasing pre-ictal symptoms (auras with sudden disequilibrium and visual fuzziness) on study days. There has been a noticeable increase in near-miss episodes with transient loss of awareness lasting a few seconds, occurring several times per week, especially on mornings following late-night revision. Teachers have raised concern about declining concentration, slowed processing speed, and missed coursework deadlines. Weight has remained stable; no intercurrent illness or head injury reported. Adherence is reported as good. No alcohol or recreational drug use. Investigations/Monitoring to Date: - Last EEG (6 months ago): non-specific diffuse fast activity; no clear lateralising features. - MRI brain (last year): unremarkable. - Recent bloods (last month): FBC, U&E, LFTs within normal limits; lamotrigine level mid-therapeutic. Plan of Action: Given the stress-related deterioration in day-to-day functioning and the increased frequency of brief lapses in awareness during the exam period, I recommend the following adjustments and supports: 1) Brivaracetam optimisation: increase to 100 mg in the morning and 125 mg at night for 1 week, then 125 mg twice daily thereafter if tolerated. Monitor for mood changes and excessive sedation. If troublesome somnolence occurs, revert to 100 mg twice daily and notify the clinic. 2) Lamotrigine: maintain 150 mg twice daily for now. If myoclonic jerks intensify or morning lapses persist after brivaracetam optimisation, we will consider a cautious increase to 175 mg twice daily at the next review. 3) Rescue strategy: retain buccal midazolam 10 mg for clusters or prolonged events; parents and school have updated care plan and know administration protocol. 4) Lifestyle and stress mitigation: strict sleep schedule with 7–8 hours nightly, avoid late-night revision sessions, schedule breaks during study, regular hydration and balanced meals. She has been referred to our neuropsychology-led stress management group and to the hospital education liaison team for exam accommodations (quiet room, rest breaks, extra time as needed). 5) Safety: reinforce seizure first aid with school/assessment centre. Avoid unsupervised swimming and heights. Consider temporary pause on driving applications until spells of altered awareness have resolved and we have clarified nature of events. 6) Further evaluation: book an ambulatory EEG during a representative study week to capture brief lapses; if non-diagnostic, proceed to short-term video-EEG telemetry. We will also obtain an updated cognitive screening profile to quantify the impact of stress on attention and processing speed. Follow-up has been arranged in 8 weeks, sooner if events escalate or any tonic-clonic seizures recur. Please advise us promptly if there are mood changes on the higher brivaracetam dose or if the brief lapses become longer or more frequent. With best wishes

Family history non-contributory by patient account. Other Medical Problems: Seasonal allergic rhinitis (OTC cetirizine as required). Mild iron deficiency previously treated; currently asymptomatic. Management Plan: - Continue sodium valproate 500 mg mane and 1000 mg nocte; maintain single brand. - Clobazam 10 mg nocte to continue for morning myoclonus; review for potential taper if stable for a further six months. - Arrange ambulatory EEG with sleep capture and repeat serum levels for valproate and full blood count/LFTs in three months. - Provide written seizure first-aid and SUDEP risk counselling; reinforce adherence and avoidance of sleep deprivation. - Because the patient lives on a houseboat with intermittent electricity, supply a battery back-up pack for phone and rescue medication reminders; pharmacy to issue a second charger and waterproof medication pouch. - Safety advice updated: avoid unsupervised swimming; shower rather than bathe; continue not to drive. - Follow-up in six months or earlier if breakthrough events occur. This 23-year-old student lives on a moored houseboat and reports occasional power outages that sometimes delay charging of her phone and medication reminder device. She keeps medications in a dry, insulated container and has not missed doses in the past two months by her account. Her parents accompany her to clinic and corroborate the recent history. Her parents report a reduction in convulsive events, with only a single tonic-clonic seizure over the past six months. Brief myoclonic jerks persist weekly on awakening but are considered tolerable. Previous routine EEG showed intermittent generalised spike–wave without clear lateralising features; classification remains under review pending ambulatory capture of awakening episodes. Bloods from last review: valproate level within target range; FBC and LFTs normal. We discussed the importance of consistent dosing times despite variable power availability. She agreed to set dual reminders (phone and wind-up alarm) and to keep a charged power bank in her go-bag. No adverse effects from current regimen besides mild morning drowsiness for 30–45 minutes, which she finds manageable with staggered waking. Yours sincerely

Since my last assessment in March 2025, her diary and a menstrual tracking app together suggest a catamenial pattern to her events, with clusters tending to occur from two days before menstruation through day three of her cycle. She has been diligent in logging symptoms, sleep times, and medication doses. Current medication at the time of review is: Levetiracetam 1000 mg twice daily, Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, and Clobazam 5 mg at night; she also uses Folic Acid 400 micrograms once daily. She previously trialled Zonisamide (discontinued in January 2025 due to appetite loss and low mood) and a brief course of Brivaracetam (stopped due to dizziness without clear benefit). She reports mild fatigue in the late afternoon but no rash, diplopia, or significant mood lability. Liver function and full blood count from July 2025 were within reference limits. Her parents accompany her today and corroborate the pattern described. Her parents report a reduction in convulsive events, with only a single tonic-clonic seizure over the past six months. Brief myoclonic jerks persist monthly on awakening but are considered tolerable. There have been no prolonged or status episodes since treatment escalation. She notes that sleep disruption the night before menses remains a consistent trigger, and she has been using phone reminders around the perimenstrual window to reinforce adherence. There have been no injuries or emergency department attendances. We discussed that, while the temporal association with her cycle is suggestive, we have not altered treatment pending further corroboration. She is agreeable to continuing her seizure and menstrual logging for another two cycles, and she has consented to share the app export with our service. She has also requested information about non-hormonal strategies for perimenstrual symptom management; I have provided written resources and signposted the epilepsy specialist nurse for practical support. She is not planning pregnancy in the next year and understands the need to contact us early if this changes. I will arrange a routine EEG with sleep deprivation and update you with the findings. For now, I have advised no medication changes and to maintain current dosing times. I will review her again in three months, sooner if there is any deterioration or recurrence of convulsive activity. Yours sincerely

Plan: - Continue Lacosamide 150 mg twice daily and Zonisamide 200 mg nocte for now. - Check Zonisamide trough level and repeat U&E/bicarbonate in 6 weeks. - Arrange ambulatory EEG to capture weekday clustering. - Occupational health referral to consider temporary workload adjustments and regular protected breaks. - Provide written seizure first-aid guidance to employer; patient to avoid lone work at heights or near open water/unguarded machinery (ï¿½). - Telephone review in 8 weeks; earlier if seizure frequency increases or any generalised events occur. I will update you following results. Please let me know if any concerns are raised by his workplace or caregivers in the interim. Yours sincerely
